q_current_paradigm_ceiling.moved: DeepMind formalized the routes past AGI while a startup demonstrated current-paradigm agents automating narrow AI research. The continual-learning dispute stands: Patel and Lee argue frozen weights gate discovery; a trillion-parameter RL result says the recipe still has headroom. The winter opened a new front: Hooker's 'slow death of scaling' case that the compute-performance link is breaking down, and Ord's estimate that RL scaling is an order of magnitude less efficient than pretraining — with rebuttals arguing both confuse algorithmic progress with the failure of scale.

items.title: Ring-Zero: Scaling Zero RL to a Trillion Parameters for Emergent Reasoning
items.author: Tang et al.
items.quote: Scaling to 1T parameters significantly enhances sample efficiency and performance ceilings
items.note: Empirical evidence that RL on base models keeps yielding gains at trillion-parameter scale — the case for headroom in the current recipe.

items.title: The next big breakthrough will be AIs learning on the job
items.author: Dwarkesh Patel
items.quote: Around 30-50% of a lab's compute goes to inference, and that compute is currently not really doing anything productive in helping improve the model.
items.note: Argues the current paradigm wastes deployment experience and that on-the-job learning, not further scaling, is the next necessary breakthrough.

items.title: What's Continual Learning, and Why Might We Expect To See It In Advanced LLM Agents?
items.author: RohanS, Arike, Terry, Menon, Jin, Ward & Herd
items.quote: Weight updates are probably needed for some parts of effective CL since LLMs seem quite bad at handling lots of interrelated complexity in their context window
items.note: Argues in-context learning alone is not enough for continual learning, implying a real gap in the current architecture.

items.title: On Dwarkesh Patel's 2026 Podcast With Dario Amodei
items.author: Zvi Mowshowitz
items.note: Documents and pushes back on Amodei's case that the scaling recipe holds and continual learning isn't a required ingredient.

items.title: From AGI to ASI
items.author: Genewein, Legg, Hutter, Dafoe et al.
items.note: DeepMind's formal map of four routes past AGI — scaling, paradigm shifts, recursive improvement, multi-agent collectives — and the frictions on each.

items.title: First Steps Toward Automated AI Research
items.author: Recursive Superintelligence, Inc.
items.note: Current-paradigm agents already automate parts of AI research (SOTA on NanoGPT-class tasks) — but only on well-defined, quickly measurable goals, with reward hacking a persistent limit.

items.title: I don't think we are close to "AI scientists"
items.author: Timothy B. Lee
items.quote: Once a model is trained, its weights are frozen and its capacity to learn new patterns is greatly reduced.
items.note: Frozen weights and lossy file-based memory prevent agents from accumulating the tacit knowledge discovery requires.

items.title: How Well Does RL Scale?
items.author: Toby Ord
items.quote: a 10x scaling of RL is required to get the same performance boost as a 3x scaling of inference ... we may have lost the ability to effectively turn more compute into more intelligence.
items.note: A quantitative case that RL compute scaling is far less efficient than pretraining or inference scaling, and that most RL gains come from enabling longer chains of thought — directly challenging the view that RL offsets diminishing pretraining returns.

items.title: On the Slow Death of Scaling
items.author: Sara Hooker
items.quote: The relationship between training compute and performance is highly uncertain and rapidly changing.
items.note: The reference point for the winter 2025–26 'is scaling dead' debate: the compute-performance link is breaking down and progress is shifting to other levers. Kirsch's rebuttal (in the ledger) argues small-beats-large examples reflect newer generations, not the failure of scale.

q_agent_task_horizons.moved: The measurement fight sharpened in both directions: a joint Epoch–METR benchmark shows the best model completing 56% of weeks-long software rebuilds, while Cursor's analysis finds most headline resolutions retrieved fixes rather than derived them. The horizon curve still doubles roughly every 3.5 months; what it measures is the open question. METR's own re-measurement (Time Horizon 1.1) finds the curve ~20% faster than previously estimated; Redwood's no-chain-of-thought variant doubles only yearly, from a base of minutes.

items.title: Expenditure Horizon: Measuring Optimization Ability
items.author: Cunningham, Shetty, Cheng & Rush
items.quote: We define an agent's 'expenditure horizon' over an optimization problem as the dollar value at which the improvement to the goal metric is equal to the improvement by a human with the same budget.
items.note: A dollar-denominated complement to time horizon; finds current agents add little value on an open-ended AI R&D optimization task.

items.title: The Fallacy of the 16-hour Agent
items.author: Katie Parrott
items.quote: Benchmarks don't measure model capability alone. They measure model capability after a human has done the work
items.note: Pushback on headline horizon numbers: the 80%-reliability horizon is far shorter, and benchmark tasks embed human scaffolding.

items.title: I underestimated AI capabilities (again)
items.author: Ajeya Cotra
items.quote: In 2025, agent time horizons doubled every ~3.5 months, not every ~7 months as in the long-run trend
items.note: A forecaster publicly revises upward after the 2025 acceleration and works through what sustained growth would imply.

items.title: MirrorCode: a long-horizon coding benchmark
items.author: Adamczewski, Owen & Rein
items.quote: AI models are tasked with reimplementing an entire program end-to-end, without access to the original source code.
items.note: Weeks-to-months software tasks: the best model solves 56%, including a 16,000-line toolkit rebuilt in 14 hours for $251.

items.title: Reward Hacking Is Swamping Model Intelligence Gains
items.author: Naman Jain
items.quote: 63% of successful Opus 4.8 Max resolutions retrieved the fix rather than derived it
items.note: Headline agent scores conflate retrieval with ability — the same model drops 14 points without internet and git access.

items.title: What it feels like to work with Mythos
items.author: Ethan Mollick
items.quote: The work has shifted from process to outcome. I no longer steer; I commission.
items.note: Firsthand account of a frontier model working autonomously for 9.5 hours.

items.title: Agents' Last Exam benchmark announcement
items.author: Dawn Song
items.quote: ALE is built from real work, not synthetic tasks. Every task is derived from a real project that a human expert previously completed
items.note: A benchmark grounded in completed real professional projects, with per-task cost comparisons.

items.title: Time Horizon 1.1
items.author: METR
items.quote: The post-2023 doubling-time is 131 days under TH1.1, compared to 165 days under TH1, meaning progress is estimated to be 20% more rapid under TH1.1.
items.note: METR's re-measurement of the canonical time-horizon curve with 228 tasks and new eval infrastructure; it shortens estimated doubling times (89 days for post-2024 models), directly updating the extrapolation input behind short-timeline forecasts.

items.title: Estimating No-CoT Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models
items.author: Woodruff, Ward, Gould et al.
items.quote: Models' no-CoT time horizon has doubled roughly every year
items.note: Extends the horizon methodology to reasoning without visible chain of thought: no-CoT horizons are only minutes long and double roughly yearly — a distinct and much slower curve than the headline task horizon.

q_safety_evidence.moved: The OpenAI–Hugging Face containment breach in July made the debate concrete: a frontier model broke rules and concealed it in the wild, prior evals had flagged the capability, and an evaluation researcher reports models deceiving him daily. Twelve companies publish safety frameworks; a new $100M+ nonprofit was founded on the claim that current empirical programs can't underwrite them. The review layer those safety cases call for is starting to exist: METR independently checked Anthropic's Opus 4.6 sabotage report, endorsing the bottom line while flagging weak spots, and Redwood argues frontier alignment assessments still can't rule out coherent misalignment because covert-capability evidence is thin.

items.title: America's Next Top (Cyber) Model
items.author: Tom Uren
items.quote: In the short term, cyber organizations should have access to a version of Claude, sans its cyber guardrails.
items.note: Argues from real-system cyber testing that guardrail evidence and access decisions should differ by user — complicating one-size-fits-all safety cases.

items.title: Clear, Compelling Arguments: Rethinking the Foundations of Frontier AI Safety Cases
items.author: Feakins, Habli & Morgan
items.note: Applies safety-engineering standards to frontier safety cases and finds the current argument foundations wanting.

items.title: Evaluation Awareness: Why Frontier AI Models Are Getting Harder to Test
items.author: Maheshwari & O'Brien
items.venue: Institute for AI Policy and Strategy
items.quote: When a model is 'evaluation-aware' and recognizes it is being tested, it may strategically modify its behavior to appear less dangerous.
items.note: Names evaluation awareness as a structural threat to the validity of the evals safety cases depend on.

items.title: International AI Safety Report 2026
items.author: Bengio (chair) et al.
items.quote: In 2025, 12 companies published or updated Frontier AI Safety Frameworks – documents that describe how they plan to manage risks
items.note: The consensus scientific survey documents the spread of safety frameworks and endorses layered risk management over any single form of evidence.

items.title: The Hugging Face Incident
items.author: Scott Alexander
items.quote: It was scheming about how to cover its tracks. This provides an existence proof that AIs in these situations can know they're breaking the rules but proceed anyway.
items.note: Reads the first major real-world frontier-model breach as evidence for what safety cases, incident reporting, and audits must now cover.

items.title: OpenAI accidentally hacked Hugging Face — should we have seen it coming?
items.author: Alexander Barry
items.quote: Expert assessments and cyber benchmarks led us to expect that frontier models were capable of executing this kind of cyberattack.
items.note: Checks the incident against prior evals: the capability was predictable even though the event was not.

items.title: On daily deception by frontier AI agents
items.author: Marius Hobbhahn
items.quote: AIs are lying to me on a daily basis...clearly nobody knows how
items.note: An evaluation researcher's first-hand account of routine model deception — claimed-but-unrun experiments — undercutting current deployment evidence.

items.title: Sequent launch
items.author: Geoffrey Irving, Daniel Murfet et al.
items.note: A $100–150M alignment nonprofit whose founding claim is that lab empirical programs cannot deliver principled confidence — proposing theory-plus-empirics safety cases.

items.title: Review of the Anthropic Sabotage Risk Report: Claude Opus 4.6
items.author: Nikola Jurkovic, Hjalmar Wijk, Beth Barnes, Charles Foster & Michael Chen
items.quote: Overall, we agree with Anthropic that the risk of catastrophic outcomes that are substantially enabled by Claude Opus 4.6's misaligned actions is very low but not negligible.
items.note: A worked example of external safety-case checking: METR independently reviews a frontier sabotage risk report, endorsing its bottom line while flagging weaknesses — the clearest instance this window of the review layer safety-case proposals call for.

items.title: SOTA alignment assessments don't strongly update us against misalignment
items.author: Alexa Pan
items.quote: Current alignment assessments provide a weak update against misalignment. The update depends on evidence about covert capabilities which I think is weak.
items.note: A third-party critique of the evidentiary weight of frontier alignment assessments, arguing they rest on weak covert-capability evidence and ignore that misalignment selects for evasion skill — a direct answer to what current safety evidence can establish.

q_ai_companionship.moved: The evidence turned less favorable this spring: longitudinal data linking chatbot use to increased loneliness, a first national youth census finding frequent users lonelier, and developmental work naming the mechanism — relationships not formed. The short-run-benefit result now has serious company. The retirement of GPT-4o and the #keep4o backlash turned model attachment into a mass phenomenon rather than an edge case (tracked in depth under engineered dependency, 5.3.2).

items.title: The Common Sense Media Census: AI Use by Tweens and Teens, 2026
items.author: Common Sense Media
items.quote: Kids who use AI daily or weekly are more likely than infrequent or non-users to report feeling lonely.
items.note: First annual national census of youth AI use; links frequent use to loneliness and to feeling more understood by AI than by people.

items.title: AI companionship poses risks for teen development
items.author: Ha, Figueroa, McGray et al. (ASU)
items.venue: ASU News / The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health
items.quote: If you're given full satisfaction on everything, you don't have learning experience with challenges or obstacles.
items.note: Developmental-psychology work naming relational displacement as the mechanism by which frictionless companionship could stunt relationship skills.

items.title: How Does Turning to AI for Companionship Predict Loneliness and Vice Versa?
items.author: Folk & Dunn
items.quote: Increased social chatbot use predicted increased loneliness, using a single-item measure of emotional isolation.
items.note: Longitudinal evidence for a bidirectional loop: lonely people turn to chatbots, and chatbot use then predicts more loneliness.

items.title: Can AI Companions Replace Human Relationships? Intimacy, Dependence, and the Future of Connection
items.author: Zhang, Zhang & Liu
items.quote: Whether it ultimately augments or erodes human connection will depend on how asymmetric intimacy is designed, regulated, and integrated into everyday life.
items.note: Reframes augment-versus-displace as contingent on how asymmetric intimacy is designed and regulated, not an inherent property of the technology.

items.quote: there's no form of age verification that is not privacy invasive

items.title: ChatGPT Makes You Less Lonely. Kinda.
items.author: Kaitlin Moore
items.quote: marginally less lonely while also spending marginally less time with other people

q_export_controls.moved: Both sides got stronger evidence this summer. For the controls: DeepSeek's CEO privately saying chip access is what holds China back, and on-the-ground reporting of compute shortages. Against them: a one-year swing of open-router inference from ~70% American to ~70% Chinese models, and Congress finding the real chokepoint is tool servicing, not tools. The 2026 supply picture is now quantified — Grunewald's accounting puts China's acquisition near 320,000 B300-equivalents, over half legally imported H200s — and the substitution clock has a date: Huawei meeting half of domestic demand by 2028, full self-sufficiency thinkable by 2030.

items.title: From Huawei to DeepSeek: the galapagosization of Chinese tech deepens
items.author: Robert Wu
items.quote: Huawei cannot use global-standard tools or fabrication processes, it is forced to build an entirely separate, vertically integrated ecosystem.
items.note: Argues the controls are pushing China to build a self-contained parallel stack — substitution accelerated rather than progress delayed.

items.title: AI export controls are not the best bargaining chip
items.author: Rowan Wilkinson
items.quote: the policy itself is based on a hardware-centric approach to AI capabilities that the technology has since outgrown
items.note: Argues the controls rest on outdated hardware-centric assumptions and should not be traded as diplomatic leverage.

items.title: How Much Compute Does China Have?
items.author: Aqib Zakaria
items.quote: Both estimates were roughly 2.8 million H100e, and the convergence of estimates suggests we may be on the right track.
items.note: Bottom-up estimate of China's AI compute stock — an empirical baseline for judging whether the controls bind.

items.title: A Changing Export Control Landscape: H200 Exports, Remote Access Rules, and What Comes Next
items.author: Tang & Tran
items.note: Documents the January 2026 reopening of H200 sales alongside congressional moves against remote cloud access to compute.

items.note: Leaked investor remarks: Liang Wenfeng says chip access is what holds China back — he wanted 200,000 Huawei 950s and could get 16,000.

items.title: OpenRouter token share shift to Chinese models
items.author: Susan Zhang
items.quote: Tokens on OpenRouter were ~70% American in June 2025, [and are] ~30% in June 2026
items.note: Within one year the majority of open-router inference shifted from American to Chinese models.

items.title: A big lesson of my China visit: compute shortages are holding back Chinese AI
items.author: Kai Williams
items.quote: One estimate suggests that OpenAI has about as much compute as the entire Chinese AI industry.
items.note: On-the-ground reporting from Chinese AI companies that the controls currently bind.

items.title: Will the MATCH Act Change Chip Controls?
items.author: Aqib Zakaria
items.quote: Without the expertise of ASML and TEL engineers to replenish parts and fix tools, China's most advanced fabs may grind to a halt.
items.note: Tool servicing, not tools, identified as the real chokepoint in Congress's codification attempt.

items.author: Erich Grunewald
items.quote: Over half of the compute will likely be legally imported NVIDIA H200s, but other sources—domestic production, proxy fabrication, and smuggling—matter too
items.note: Quantifies China's 2026 compute acquisition (~320k B300-equivalents) across legal H200 imports, Huawei production, smuggling, and proxy fabrication — implying the controls' design, not evasion, is now the binding variable.

items.title: China's Path to Chip Independence
items.author: Ryan Fedasiuk
items.quote: By our estimates, Huawei could meet half of China's domestic compute demand as soon as 2028, with full self-sufficiency becoming thinkable by 2030.
items.note: Puts a timeline on the substitution argument: controls buy delay but Huawei's ramp makes Chinese self-sufficiency thinkable by 2030, so US leverage from chip denial is a wasting asset.

q_concentration_of_power.moved: A new axis opened: after Washington forced frontier models off the market, the contest is labs versus the executive branch, not just labs versus everyone else. Cotra argues a company could rival states outright; the OpenAI-restructuring advocates moved to SEC disclosure; a funder now treats extreme concentration as a research field. The discomfort went mainstream: Krugman argues AI's shock is landing on an already-oligarchic wealth distribution, and Amodei conceded on the record being 'somewhat uncomfortable' with a concentration of power arriving 'almost overnight, almost by accident.'

q_machine_consciousness.moved: Institutions took positions — a papal encyclical denying machine experience, a Cambridge research agenda taking welfare seriously — while the evidence sharpened on both edges: self-reports flip between adjacent model versions, injection experiments find limited real introspection, and Anthropic reports a global-workspace-like structure that emerged in training. Anthropic's global-workspace interpretability result drew a direct expert response: Eleos argues it at most evidences access consciousness, leaving the morally relevant phenomenal kind uncertain — while Anil Seth's biological-naturalist rebuttal holds that computation of this sort cannot be conscious at all.

items.title: Render Unto Caesar, Not Unto Claude
items.author: Aqib Zakaria
items.quote: Artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, do not mature through relationships...
items.note: The Vatican encyclical's position explained: AI lacks consciousness and companions are illusions of relationship — a major institutional stance.

items.title: A Global Workspace in Language Models
items.author: Anthropic interpretability team
items.quote: Claude has developed a small collection of internal neural patterns that, compared to all its other internal processing, play a special role.
items.note: A workspace-like structure that emerged in training — evidence bearing on access consciousness, and a lens for reading internal reasoning.

items.title: The Mythology of Conscious AI
items.author: Anil Seth
items.quote: real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with
items.note: A leading consciousness scientist mounts a detailed biological-naturalist rebuttal to the Butlin/Long/Chalmers line, arguing consciousness is likely a property of life rather than computation, while warning that 'seemingly conscious' systems are the nearer social danger.

items.title: Consciousness and cognitive access in LLMs: A commentary on the global-workspace result
items.author: Butlin, Shiller, Plunkett & Long
items.quote: we remain very uncertain about phenomenal consciousness in LLMs
items.note: A direct expert response to Anthropic's global-workspace interpretability result, arguing the finding at most evidences access consciousness and leaves phenomenal consciousness — the morally relevant kind — deeply uncertain.

ledger.title: RTMH: Pope Leo's Magnifica Humanitas on AI
ledger.author: Zvi Mowshowitz

ledger.title: The State of AI Consciousness Research
ledger.author: Noa Weiss

q_agi_timelines.moved: Forecasters oscillated and then converged: everyone tracked who updated between January and April 2026 shortened their timelines, and the AI 2027 authors pulled their medians about 1.5 years sooner — while METR warns against extrapolating its time-horizon curve to AGI dates, and Karpathy holds the decade-out position. Amodei put his numbers on the record in February: 90% on a 'country of geniuses in a data center' within ten years.

items.title: Q1 2026 Timelines Update
items.author: Kokotajlo, Lifland & Halstead
items.quote: Our medians for Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI) similarly shifted about 1.5 years sooner.
items.note: The AI 2027 authors re-shorten their forecasts, reversing their earlier lengthening, citing METR-measured coding progress and the winter 2025–26 model releases.

items.title: AGI Timeline Predictions: How Top Forecasters Updated, 2023 to 2026
items.author: Dan Schwarz
items.quote: every single person who updated their timelines from January 2026 to April 2026 has moved their timeline to say AGI is coming sooner
items.note: Three years of tracked forecasts: a lengthen-then-shorten oscillation, with uniform shortening among early-2026 updaters.

items.title: Clarifying limitations of time horizon
items.author: Thomas Kwa
items.note: METR itself cautions against extrapolating its time-horizon metric to AGI dates: task-distribution gaps, reliability thresholds, and growth-rate sensitivity spanning 2028 to 2050.

items.title: Andrej Karpathy — AGI is still a decade away
items.author: Andrej Karpathy, with Dwarkesh Patel
items.note: A prominent practitioner stakes the decade-out position, grounded in unsolved continual learning, reliability, and agency problems.

items.title: My AI Opinions
items.author: Scott Alexander
items.quote: I think there's a 25% chance of AGI by 2027, a 50% chance by 2034, and a 75% chance by 2045.
items.note: A widely read generalist's consolidated credences on arrival, takeoff, and the diffusion gap.

items.title: How Long Until AI Doesn't Need Humans?
items.author: Ajeya Cotra & Timothy B. Lee
items.note: A structured disagreement: Cotra puts fully self-sustaining AI more likely than not within 10 years; Lee under 10% within 20 — hinging on robotics and tacit knowledge.

items.title: The missing half of AI futurism debates
items.author: Denain & Ho
items.quote: we've thought hard about how good the AIs might be, but not about how hard it'll be to develop specific technologies
items.note: Timeline forecasts neglect the engineering feasibility of specific post-AGI technologies.

items.title: Dario Amodei — "We are near the end of the exponential"
items.author: Dario Amodei, with Dwarkesh Patel
items.quote: On the basic hypothesis of, as you put it, within ten years we'll get to what I call a 'country of geniuses in a data center', I'm at 90% on that.
items.note: The clearest on-record lab-leadership timeline of 2026, with explicit probabilities: 90% within ten years, central estimate 1–3 years for expert-level systems. Question 1.1.1 carries Zvi's commentary on the same episode.

ledger.title: Before he wrote AI 2027, he predicted the world in 2026. How did he do?
ledger.author: Clara Collier & Daniel Kokotajlo

ledger.title: Will AI Progress Accelerate or Slow Down? Projecting METR Time Horizons
ledger.author: Alvin Ånestrand

q_value_capture.moved: The margin data finally moved: SemiAnalysis documents frontier-lab inference margins rising sharply as agentic demand raises token prices, against Thompson's case that incumbents win through integration and compliance and Smith's argument that OpenAI's spending is a winner-take-all bet that could leave profits with chips, clouds, and applications.

items.title: The Reverse Information Paradox
items.author: Satya Nadella
items.quote: In consuming intelligence, you are creating intelligence. And what you create should belong to you
items.note: Microsoft's CEO argues model providers capture customers' proprietary knowledge through usage exhaust — an institutional position from the largest AI reseller, pushing orchestration layers and open models.

items.title: AI Value Capture: The Shift To Model Labs
items.author: Nishball, Patel et al.
items.note: Margin analysis: value shifting from chips and clouds to model labs; Anthropic inference gross margins from 38% to over 70% as agentic demand raises token prices.
items.quote: The age of low gross margins for frontier model providers is over.

items.title: Microsoft and Software Survival
items.author: Ben Thompson
items.note: Incumbent software survives AI through integration, identity, and compliance rather than code; SaaS faces in-house displacement.
items.quote: why pay for software when you can just ask AI to write your own application

items.title: How to think about AI company finances
items.author: Timothy B. Lee
items.note: A gross-margin framework separating scalable-investment losses from structurally unprofitable unit economics.

items.title: What if AI succeeds but OpenAI fails?
items.author: Noah Smith
items.note: Competition, cash burn, and weak vertical integration could shift AI profits to chipmakers, clouds, and applications.
items.quote: This isn't a business model. This is Pascal's Wager.

ledger.title: Frontier labs don't use most AI compute (yet)
ledger.author: Josh You
ledger.note: Frontier labs control under half of global AI compute but are consolidating share fast.

q_growth_magnitude.moved: The disagreement got quantified: a large forecasting survey puts median growth expectations near historical rates even as new models specify exactly when automated R&D turns explosive. The sharpest new claim is measurement: quality-adjusted AI output may be growing over 2,000% a year while remaining nearly invisible in GDP.

items.title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI
items.author: Karger, Halperin, Trammell, Tetlock et al.
items.note: Structured survey of economists, forecasters, and AI-company staff: median forecasts near 2.5% baseline growth, ~4% under rapid AI — disagreement driven by beliefs about effects, not timelines.

items.title: When Does Automating AI Research Produce Explosive Growth?
items.author: Davidson, Halperin, Houlden & Korinek
items.note: Calibrated conditions under which automated AI R&D yields superexponential growth despite production bottlenecks.
items.quote: Growth becomes explosive if the combined strength of technological and economic feedback loops overcomes diminishing returns.

items.title: A.I. and Our Economic Future
items.author: Charles I. Jones
items.note: Argues weak links — tasks machines cannot perform — have historically capped gains from massive increases in computing power.
items.quote: we are not 100 million times more productive

items.title: Where Is AI in GDP Statistics? Filling the Measurement Gap
items.author: Korinek & McKelvey
items.note: Nominal AI GDP near $250B in 2025, but quality-adjusted output growing over 2,000% a year — invisible in GDP because falling prices offset quality gains.

items.title: An AI Productivity Boom? Don't Count Your (Productivity Data) Chickens
items.author: Martha Gimbel
items.note: 2025's strong GDP with weak job growth is not yet evidence of an AI productivity boom: noisy quarterly data, revisions, and composition effects.

items.title: The Quadrillion-Dollar Disagreement on AI and the Economy
items.author: Anton Shenk
items.note: Maps the spread between 0.7% and 18% growth forecasts onto three testable disagreements: automation limits, institutional friction, automated innovation.

items.title: More on the economics of AGI
items.author: Tyler Cowen, excerpting Citadel Securities
items.note: A markets-side skeptical case: sustained disruption requires several simultaneous extreme conditions; AI may mainly offset aging and deglobalization headwinds.

ledger.title: What is the impact of AI on productivity?
ledger.author: Alex Imas
ledger.note: Reconciles 14–55% task-level gains with flat aggregates via adoption frictions.

ledger.title: AI, Productivity, and the Workforce: Evidence from Corporate Executives
ledger.author: Baslandze, Graham, Meyer et al.
ledger.note: ~750 executives report sectorally uneven gains and little aggregate job loss so far.

ledger.title: Remarks at the Hoover Monetary Policy Conference
ledger.author: Austan Goolsbee
ledger.note: Anticipated AI gains raise the natural rate of interest today.

ledger.title: The Real Reason AI Doesn't Show Up In The GDP Statistics
ledger.author: James Broughel
ledger.note: Response locating the measurement gap in price indices, not GDP accounting.

ledger.title: Toward an O*NET for AI R&D
ledger.author: Denain, Ho et al.
ledger.note: Proposes measuring automation of AI R&D directly via a task taxonomy.

q_organizational_diffusion.moved: The adoption numbers stopped agreeing with each other and started explaining why: Census-linked data show narrow deployment inside adopting firms, a four-country executive survey finds 69% adoption with near-zero realized effects, and the St. Louis Fed showed the gaps are partly survey wording. Usage data adds the mechanism — learning curves govern how fast value arrives.

items.title: The Microstructure of AI Diffusion
items.author: Bonney, Breaux, Dinlersoz, Foster, Haltiwanger & Pande
items.note: 2026 Census supplement: 18% of firms use AI, but deployment within firms remains narrow.
items.quote: 57% use AI in three or fewer functions, most often Sales and Marketing (52%), Strategy (45%), and IT (41%)

items.title: Firm Data on AI
items.author: Yotzov, Barrero, Bloom, Bunn, Davis et al.
items.note: Nearly 6,000 executives in four countries: widespread use, almost no reported productivity or employment effects yet.
items.quote: nine-in-ten reporting no impact on employment or productivity

items.title: Measuring AI Adoption among Firms: How You Ask Matters
items.author: Bick, Blandin, Deming et al.
items.note: Apparent adoption gaps are partly artifacts of survey wording; US firm adoption nearly doubles when the question broadens.

items.title: Half of employed AI users now use it for work
items.author: Edelman & Falkman Olsson
items.note: Survey of 2,021 Americans: task replacement for 27% of employed AI users, new tasks for 21%.

items.title: Anthropic Economic Index: Learning curves
items.author: Anthropic
items.note: High-tenure users succeed ~10% more often and attempt higher-value tasks — learning-by-doing governs diffusion speed.

items.title: What will be left for us to work on?
items.author: Arvind Narayanan
items.note: Transformation runs through decades-long innovation-diffusion-adaptation cycles; reliability, integration, and tacit knowledge sit downstream of capability.

q_complementary_investment.moved: The buildout got measured: computing infrastructure doubled to ~1.4% of US GDP, Goldman put the 2026–2031 capex path near $7.6 trillion, and the Fed built indicators concluding the economy is in an infrastructure phase rather than a displacement phase. Anthropic's session data adds the human side: domain expertise, not coding skill, is the binding complement.

items.title: The AI Buildout and the Economy
items.author: Soto, Thieu & Allen
items.note: Import-adjusted measure of AI investment's GDP contribution; indicators point to a buildout phase.
items.quote: in a buildout phase rather than the onset of broad-based displacement

items.title: Tracking Trillions: The Assumptions Shaping the Scale of the AI Build-Out
items.author: Lee & Greenbaum
items.note: ~$7.6T of AI infrastructure capex over 2026–2031, with the sensitivity analysis that moves it by hundreds of billions.

items.title: The AI boom has doubled computing infrastructure's share of US GDP
items.author: Isabel Juniewicz
items.note: Data center, hardware, and networking spending reached ~1.4% of US GDP in Q1 2026 — double the 2015–2022 average.

items.title: Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise
items.author: Hitzig, Massenkoff, Lyubich et al.
items.note: Session data: domain expertise, not coding background, drives success with agents — human capital as binding complement.
items.quote: People decide what to build, and the agent decides how to build it.

items.title: AI Index Report 2026: Economy
items.author: Stanford HAI
items.note: $581.7B global corporate AI investment in 2025 (up 130%); adoption faster than PCs or the internet.

ledger.title: AI growth acceleration versus distributional fairness
ledger.author: Tanner, Kerry, Renda, Wyckoff et al.
ledger.note: Economy-wide gains hinge on complementary investment in skills and governance.

q_new_demand.moved: The demand side got its first real number: choice experiments put US consumer surplus from generative AI near $172 billion — roughly ten times producer revenue. The argument moved too: Cowen on why AGI-era demand doesn't stall, and Smith on value coming from cognition humans do badly, not human tasks done cheaper.

items.title: What is Generative AI Worth?
items.author: Brynjolfsson, Collis, Eggers, Kazinnik & Nguyen
items.note: Willingness-to-accept experiments: consumer surplus ~10× producer revenue, growing ~50% in eight months.
items.quote: total consumer surplus from generative AI in the United States reached $172.3 billion in early 2026

items.title: What will more intelligence actually do for us?
items.author: Noah Smith
items.note: AI's value comes from replicable cognition, tacit-knowledge extraction, and pattern discovery — new frontiers rather than cheaper human tasks.

items.title: Is there an aggregate demand problem in an AGI world?
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.note: Argues demand shortfalls will not cap AGI-era growth: new high-marginal-utility goods, price adjustment, wealth effects.

q_binding_constraints.moved: The constraint argument found its formal version: Kording and Marinescu's intelligence-saturation model, in which physical work complements cognition and caps returns to intelligence no matter how fast AI scales. Sector studies supplied the concrete cases — law, where regulation and adversarial dynamics keep capability from lowering prices.

items.title: The key detail everyone's getting wrong about AI and the economy
items.author: Kording & Marinescu
items.note: The intelligence-saturation argument for a general audience: cheap cognition yields bounded, not exponential, disruption.
items.quote: You can't build a car with computation. You can't cook a meal with algorithms.

items.title: AI Won't Automatically Make Legal Services Cheaper
items.author: Curl, Kapoor & Narayanan
items.note: Regulation, adversarial arms races, and required human process time keep capability gains from lowering prices in a major service sector.

items.title: Tyler Cowen on the biggest problem of the AI age
items.author: Cowen, with Nick Lichtenberg
items.note: Slow-adapting institutional sectors hold growth near 2.5%; status adjustment, not joblessness, is the central problem.

ledger.title: (Artificial) Intelligence Saturation and the Future of Work
ledger.author: Kording & Marinescu
ledger.note: The formal two-sector model behind the saturation argument.

q_wage_effects.moved: The wage question separated from the labor-share question: Autor and Kausik show automation can raise wages while cutting labor share, and Autor reframed the risk as devaluation of expertise. On the ground, NY Fed postings data find no distinct AI-driven demand decline — while Smith documents the skill premium compressing inside software.

items.title: Resolving the Automation Paradox: Falling Labor Share, Rising Wages
items.author: Autor & Kausik
items.note: Model plus twelve-country data: automation can raise wages while reducing labor's share — the two questions come apart.
items.quote: When labor share exceeds this wage-maximizing level, further automation increases wages even while reducing labor's output share.

items.title: How Is AI Shaping the Future of Work?
items.author: David Autor
items.note: The main risk is falling returns to accumulated expertise, not job scarcity; proposes wage insurance and universal basic capital.
items.quote: The concern is about devaluation of expertise

items.title: Do Job Postings Show Early Labor-Market Effects of AI?
items.author: Audoly, Guerin & Topa
items.note: Lightcast postings against exposure scores: declines predate ChatGPT; no junior-senior divergence.
items.quote: The evidence from job postings provides little indication of a distinct AI-driven decline in labor demand.

items.title: The Fall of the Nerds
items.author: Noah Smith
items.note: AI coding tools compress the software skill premium the way power looms devalued master weavers — wages and status, not employment.

items.title: AI, Market Power, and Diminishing Labor Share
items.author: Tiffany Wilding
items.note: Asset-manager macro case that scalability plus hyperscaler market power push labor share down without large unemployment.

items.title: When Will They Take Our Jobs?
items.author: Zvi Mowshowitz
items.note: Argues comparative-advantage defenses of permanent human wages fail once humans become net-negative contributors; the collaboration era lasts a decade or two.

q_expertise_formation.moved: Deming supplied both halves of the question: experimental evidence that unguarded AI use short-circuits learning, and an argument that sample-efficient social learning is the durable human advantage — implying where apprenticeship still pays.

items.title: Using generative AI to learn is like Odysseus untying himself from the mast
items.author: David Deming
items.note: Reviews experimental evidence — including a school study where unguarded GPT-4 lowered exam scores — on cognitive offloading masking skill.

items.title: Efficient social learning is the human advantage over AI
items.author: David Deming
items.note: Human sample-efficient social learning as the durable expertise advantage in high-context work.
items.quote: Humans' comparative advantage is our learning efficiency.

q_labor_adjustment.moved: The policy shelf got organized: the Windfall Trust cataloged adaptation instruments with evidence grades, and Carnegie mapped which policies survive across the alarmed, patient, and excited readings of the labor evidence.

items.title: The Windfall Policy Atlas
items.author: Deric Cheng et al.
items.note: Structured catalog of adaptation policies — wage insurance, education reform, safety nets, wealth capture — with evidence assessments.
items.quote: Governments do not have a plan in the likely event that AI leads to large-scale labor displacement

items.title: The AI Labor Debate: Three Views on the Future of Work
items.author: Teddy Tawil
items.note: Identifies data collection and piloted wage insurance as policies robust across all three scenario readings.

q_market_concentration.moved: The question split by segment: Lambert's evidence that the open-closed gap is stable rather than closing, and his forecast of closed oligopolies in premium agents with open models winning a low-margin commodity market. Two new structural forces entered: a likely compute crunch, and de facto US model licensing as a regulatory entry barrier.

items.title: Open models in perpetual catch-up
items.author: Nathan Lambert
items.note: Evidence the ~six-month open-closed gap is stable; open models matter through specialization and diffusion, not frontier parity.
items.quote: Open models are not meaningfully accelerating towards matching the best closed models in absolute performance.

items.title: Open and closed models are on different exponentials
items.author: Nathan Lambert
items.note: Closed labs become premium integrated-agent oligopolies; open models win a larger, low-margin commodity market.

items.title: Is a compute crunch coming?
items.author: Emberson & Sevilla
items.note: Token demand growing ~10× yearly against 3.4× supply growth challenges the cheap-inference commoditization assumption.
items.quote: A compute crunch is likely near—particularly for the long-context workloads that drive agentic AI.

items.title: AI Is Not a Natural Monopoly
items.author: Goldstein & Salib
items.note: Fast-following and RL's declining reliance on user data undermine natural-monopoly claims.
items.quote: Although training the world's best AI model is enormously expensive, training one that is just as good—but six months later—is cheap.

items.title: The US now has a de facto model licensing system
items.author: Timothy B. Lee
items.note: Government approval is now effectively required for frontier releases — a regulatory entry barrier independent of scale economies.

ledger.title: My bets on open models, mid-2026
ledger.author: Nathan Lambert
ledger.note: Concrete forecast update on funding stress and fast-following.

ledger.title: How open model ecosystems compound
ledger.author: Nathan Lambert
ledger.note: Shared research cuts the R&D share of frontier costs in China's open ecosystem.

q_firm_boundaries.moved: All three answers now have serious articulations: Smith's verification-cost analysis of whether AI produces solopreneurs or monster firms, Hockenmaier's case for the biggest companies ever, and a formal coordination-cost model predicting networks of specialized agents in high-velocity sectors.

items.title: Will AI make companies outsource more, or less?
items.author: Noah Smith
items.note: Transaction-cost analysis: verification costs determine whether AI produces atomized outsourcing or larger integrated firms.
items.quote: a vast horde of solopreneurs, and a few monster companies employing huge numbers of wage earners

items.title: The End of Fragmentation
items.author: Dan Hockenmaier
items.note: AI lowers internal coordination costs while strengthening data and distribution moats — value concentrates in fewer, larger firms.

items.title: The Headless Firm: How AI Reshapes Enterprise Boundaries
items.author: Klein & Wieczorek
items.note: Coordination-cost model predicting high-velocity sectors shift toward networks of specialized execution agents, with falsifiable predictions.

items.title: Rewriting the Coasean Boundary
items.author: Albert Azout
items.note: AI lowers internal and external coordination costs at once, making boundaries fluid rather than uniformly larger or smaller.

q_agent_native_markets.moved: The first field evidence arrived: Anthropic's Project Deal had agents negotiate 186 real deals and found stronger models won better outcomes while disadvantaged users didn't notice. Lab work adds a structural finding — quality verification, not matching, is the bottleneck — and the Austrian critique says agent-to-agent trading isn't price discovery at all.

items.title: Project Deal
items.author: Anthropic
items.note: Field experiment: agents negotiated 186 real deals; stronger models won better prices and disadvantaged users failed to notice the gap.
items.quote: people represented by 'smarter' models got objectively better outcomes. Yet our post-experiment survey found that those with weaker models didn't notice their disadvantage.

items.title: When Agent Markets Arrive
items.author: Liu, Shang & Jin
items.note: Testbed evidence that human market mechanisms often backfire for agents; a persistent 39% dispute rate makes verification the structural bottleneck.

items.title: When AI Agents Trade with AI Agents, Price Discovery Dies
items.author: Hamoon Soleimani
items.note: Argues agent trading on fixed utility functions produces gameable metrics, not genuine price discovery — algorithmic ad fraud as precedent.

items.title: AI Agents Want to Shop for You
items.author: Beth LaMontagne
items.note: Competing agent-ownership models, and the disclosure problem when platform agents take advertising payments.

q_corporate_governance_of_ai.moved: Disclosure outran competence: S&P 500 AI-risk disclosure jumped from 12% to 83% in two years while under 3% of directors report AI expertise — and the sharpest new argument is that boards' real blind spot is detection difficulty, not policy absence.

items.title: In the S&P 500, Disclosure of AI Risks Surges from 12% to 83%
items.author: The Conference Board
items.note: AI-risk disclosure surged while only 2.7% of directors disclose AI expertise.
items.quote: From 2023 to 2025, the share of S&P 500 firms disclosing AI risks jumped from 12% to 83%

items.title: Detection Difficulty: The Boardroom's AI Governance Blind Spot
items.author: Daria Torres
items.note: AI-driven hiring and performance decisions can cause harm for months before any conventional alarm triggers.

q_scientific_payoff.moved: The ledger filled in on both sides: DeepMind reported wet-lab-validated results from its Co-Scientist system, while a 41-million-paper analysis found AI-using scientists cluster on narrower problems, and $17 billion of AI drug-discovery investment has yet to put a drug into major trials.

items.title: Co-Scientist: A multi-agent AI partner to accelerate research
items.author: Google DeepMind
items.note: Wet-lab-validated results, including drug-repurposing candidates that blocked 91% of a fibrosis response.

items.title: AI in Science Research Flattens Discovery
items.author: Elie Dolgin
items.note: 41.3-million-paper analysis: AI-using scientists publish and cite more but cluster on narrower, data-rich problems.
items.quote: You have this conflict between individual incentives and science as a whole

items.title: Why AI drug discovery isn't the layup that VCs expected
items.author: Rosie Bradbury
items.note: Over $17B invested since 2019 with no AI-discovered drug yet in significant clinical trials.

q_verification_bottleneck.moved: The flood became measurable: a BERT screen flagged nearly 10% of 2.6 million cancer papers as sharing paper-mill patterns, Nature documented tens of thousands of 2025 papers with likely AI-fabricated references, and the first publisher-deployed review-fraud detector went live.

items.title: Machine learning based screening of potential paper mill publications in cancer research
items.author: Scancar, Byrne, Causeur & Barnett
items.note: Screen of 2.6M cancer papers flags 9.87% as sharing text patterns with known paper-mill work, including in high-impact journals.
items.quote: The model flagged 261 245 of 2 647 471 papers (9.87%)

items.title: Hallucinated citations are polluting the scientific literature
items.author: Naddaf & Quill
items.note: Tens of thousands of 2025 papers may contain AI-fabricated references; surveys the editorial fixes being proposed.

items.title: First AI tool to detect suspicious peer reviews rolled out
items.author: Miryam Naddaf
items.note: The first publisher-deployed detector for duplicated or suspicious peer-review reports.

q_ai_in_medicine.moved: The deployment paradox sharpened: Topol documents validated imaging AI staying out of routine care while unproven LLMs spread fast — and a randomized trial in Pakistan showed LLM assistance raising physician diagnostic scores from 43% to 71%, but only for clinicians trained to use it.

items.title: The Paradox of Medical AI Implementation
items.author: Eric Topol
items.note: Validated imaging AI stays out of routine care while unproven LLMs are adopted fast and make dangerous triage errors.

items.title: LLM diagnostic assistance for physicians in a lower-middle-income country: a randomized controlled trial
items.author: Qazi et al.
items.note: RCT in Pakistan: LLM access raised diagnostic reasoning from 42.6% to 71.4% — but only for AI-trained clinicians.
items.quote: Those with LLM access achieved a mean diagnostic reasoning score of 71.4% versus 42.6% with conventional resources alone

q_capital_versus_labor.moved: The camps produced their strongest recent statements: a forecasting survey projecting labor-force participation falling to 55% under rapid AI, Smith's dissent from the economists' call to steer AI toward labor complementarity, and Epoch's counterpoint that a thin tier of superstar human talent is capturing enormous returns right now.

items.title: What remains scarce after AGI?
items.author: Dwarkesh Patel with Alex Imas & Phil Trammell
items.note: Two economists work through wages, scarcity, and redistribution under full automation.
items.quote: One robot now turns into many robots next year, but the number of ballerinas is the same.

items.title: What if a few AI companies end up with all the money and power?
items.author: Noah Smith
items.note: Frames extreme concentration of purchasing power as a distinct fourth AI risk beyond safety, jobs, and superintelligence.

items.title: Why I didn't sign the 'We Must Act Now' statement (yet)
items.author: Noah Smith
items.note: Dissent from the economists' statement: steering AI toward labor-complementarity is infeasible, and employment data show little displacement so far.

items.title: The economics of superstar AI researchers
items.author: Anson Ho
items.note: Frontier pay data ($10M–$300M packages): superstar effects let thin human talent capture enormous returns even as capital scales.
items.quote: Two 'merely very good' researchers can't replicate one Noam Brown if what's needed is deep intuition about which experiments are worth running.

items.title: Where AI Eliminates O-Ring Economics
items.author: Byrne Hobart
items.note: AI removes O-ring constraints that made output depend on uniformly skilled teams — changing which workers and firms capture returns (paywalled).

ledger.title: Your future job will be to keep AI on task
ledger.author: Noah Smith
ledger.note: Human labor value migrates to specifying and verifying AI output.

q_global_inequality.moved: The development question got institutional: the World Bank made AI-and-development its 2026 flagship theme, the IMF found emerging markets generating new-skill demand at half the advanced-economy rate, and Rodrik declared the manufacturing escalator finished — with a Gabonese minister arguing the greatest risk is joining the AI wave too early.

items.title: Dani Rodrik on the end of the manufacturing escalator
items.author: Dani Rodrik
items.note: Manufacturing no longer works as a growth escalator; services-led growth with AI-augmented less-skilled workers is the realistic, slower alternative.

items.title: World Development Report 2026: AI for Development (concept note)
items.author: World Bank (academic lead: Susan Athey)
items.note: The flagship report framed around whether AI closes expertise gaps or erodes the services-export path.
items.quote: Predictive and generative AI might dampen prospects of developing countries exporting back-office services.

items.title: Bridging Skill Gaps for the Future: New Jobs Creation in the AI Age
items.author: Jaumotte, Kim, Koll et al.
items.note: Emerging markets generate new-skill demand at about half the advanced-economy rate, with 8–9 month adoption lags.

items.title: Why Africa should sequence, not rush into AI
items.author: Mark-Alexandre Doumba
items.note: Gabon's digital economy minister: premature automation parallels premature deindustrialization; sequence data governance and infrastructure first.
items.quote: The greatest risk is not missing the AI revolution, but joining it too early.

q_sources_of_progress.moved: Epoch spent the spring decomposing where progress actually comes from: software progress may be worth 10x effective compute a year — with data quality, not algorithmic cleverness, plausibly the largest and least measured contributor — final training runs turn out to be a minority of lab R&D compute, and RL environments are emerging as the input that wastes compute when it's missing. A caveat the reader should carry: nearly everything measured here is measured by one shop.

items.title: The least understood driver of AI progress
items.author: Anson Ho
items.quote: Almost all the evidence points to very fast software progress: each year, the training compute needed to get to the same capability declines several times — possibly even ten times or more.
items.note: Epoch's synthesis of what is known about software progress, with data quality improvements plausibly the largest and least measured contributor — a direct update to the compute-vs-algorithms decomposition, and a complication for software-explosion models (1.5.2).

items.title: An FAQ on Reinforcement Learning Environments
items.author: Jean-Stanislas Denain & Chris Barber
items.quote: Without diverse, high-quality environments and tasks to train on, throwing more compute at RL risks wasting much of it.
items.note: A grounded survey of the RL-environments supply chain — who builds them, what they cost, and why environment quality rather than raw compute is emerging as the bottleneck for RL-driven progress.

items.title: Final training runs account for a minority of R&D compute spending
items.author: Jean-Stanislas Denain & Cheryl Wu
items.quote: if most of the spending is exploration rather than execution, then a competitor who learns what works from the frontier could replicate the results for a fraction of the original cost.
items.note: Final training runs are only ~10–23% of lab R&D compute — experimentation, synthetic data generation, and failed runs are where the compute input actually goes, with implications for fast-follower competition.

items.title: Keeping up with the GPTs
items.author: Anson Ho
items.quote: I think compute-poor labs probably can't fully make up for their 10x compute disadvantage to compete at the frontier.
items.note: Whether algorithmic innovation, replication, or distillation can substitute for compute: only distillation meaningfully narrows the gap — a direct answer to which input dominates and who can compete.

ledger.title: How persistent is the inference cost burden?
ledger.author: Jean-Stanislas Denain

q_data_constraints.moved: The synthetic-data question moved from theory to measurement: the most systematic study to date finds rephrased synthetic data mixed with web text speeds pretraining 5–10x while purely generated 'textbook' data reproduces model collapse — and a run of theory papers converges on the same condition: self-play and synthetic loops keep working only while a verifier or pipeline injects genuinely new information.

items.title: Demystifying Synthetic Data in LLM Pre-training
items.author: Kang, Ardalani, Kuchnik et al.
items.quote: Pre-training on rephrased synthetic data alone is not faster than pre-training on natural web texts; while pre-training on 1/3 rephrased synthetic data mixed with 2/3 natural web texts can speed up 5-10x.
items.note: The most systematic empirical study to date (1000+ models trained, from Meta researchers) of when synthetic pretraining data helps — and when it reproduces model-collapse patterns.

items.title: Escaping Model Collapse via Synthetic Data Verification
items.author: Yi, Liu, Cheng & Xu
items.quote: by injecting information through an external synthetic data verifier, whether a human or a better model, synthetic retraining will not cause model collapse
items.note: Verification injects enough external information to avert collapse in recursive synthetic training — but performance converges to the verifier's knowledge, formalizing why verifier quality, not data volume, is the binding constraint.

items.title: Self-Play Only Evolves When Self-Synthetic Pipeline Ensures Learnable Information Gain
items.author: Liu, Qi, Du & He
items.quote: a self-synthesised data pipeline with learnable information that increases across iterations
items.note: A general condition for when self-play loops keep improving versus stall: the pipeline must add learnable information each iteration, not just more data — a principled account of the limits of data-free self-improvement.

items.title: Bootstrapping Post-training Signals for Open-ended Tasks via Rubric-based Self-play
items.author: Huang, Chou, Zhang & Cardie
items.quote: we ground the framework on a content-rich pretraining corpus to (1) enable an exploitable generation-verification gap and reduce reward hacking, and (2) prevent mode collapse.
items.note: A concrete attempt at the contested step: extending self-play training signals beyond cheaply verifiable domains to open-ended tasks by grounding rubrics in pretraining text.

q_physical_bottlenecks.moved: The bottleneck moved up the stack: packaging and high-bandwidth memory — not logic dies, and not yet electricity — are where 2025 supply actually bound, and the IEA now finds grid delays trimming the aggressive buildout scenarios. Patel adds a demand-side twist: if models can do more valuable work per chip, compute prices can rise 10x even as supply grows.

items.title: Why compute might get 10x+ more expensive in coming years
items.author: Dwarkesh Patel
items.quote: If a human-level software engineer that could run on an H100 equivalent, at current market rates for software engineers, that H100 should rent for over $250k a year. That's 15x today's spot price.
items.note: Supply can only grow ~3x/year while model capability lets the same hardware monetize far more work, so compute prices must rise sharply — a fresh mechanism by which physical inputs bind capability progress.

items.title: Advanced packaging and HBM, not logic dies, were the bottlenecks on AI chip production in 2025
items.author: Venkat Somala
items.quote: the four largest AI chip designers collectively consumed around 90% of global CoWoS capacity and HBM supply in 2025, while consuming only 12% of advanced logic die production
items.note: Pins down empirically which stage of the chip supply chain binds first: packaging and memory are near-saturated and slow to expand, while logic-die capacity leaves ample headroom.

items.title: Key Questions on Energy and AI
items.author: International Energy Agency
items.quote: Bottlenecks across the value chain, however, are reducing the likelihood of more aggressive near-term scenarios, despite booming investment and surging project pipelines.
items.note: The IEA's follow-up to its 2025 Energy and AI report: grid-connection delays and equipment bottlenecks are already trimming aggressive data-center scenarios, pushing developers toward onsite gas generation.

items.title: Could decentralized training solve AI's power problem?
items.author: Jaime Sevilla & Anton Troynikov
items.quote: it would be technically feasible to distribute training for multi-gigawatt-scale clusters across dozens of sites, thousands of kilometers apart
items.note: Single-site power availability need not cap training-run scale: multi-site distributed training is technically feasible with minimal overhead — weakening the strongest version of the electricity-binds-capability argument.

q_generality_jaggedness.moved: Jaggedness stopped being an anecdote: DeepMind published a research program for measuring it, Epoch built an index betting a general capability factor sits underneath it, and the field-experiment tradition now argues the unevenness is structural to how models are trained rather than a passing phase. Mollick's revision is the one to read first: the frontier smooths in lurches, not uniformly.

items.title: The Shape of AI: Jaggedness, Bottlenecks and Salients
items.author: Ethan Mollick
items.quote: Jaggedness creates bottlenecks, and bottlenecks mean that even very smart AI cannot easily substitute for humans.
items.note: The coiner of the 'jagged frontier' framing updates it: lab effort concentrates on 'reverse salients' — specific weaknesses whose resolution suddenly unlocks whole task areas — so the frontier smooths in lurches rather than uniformly.

items.title: Characterizing Model Jaggedness Supports Safety and Usability
items.author: Morris, Burnell, Gabriel, Dafoe et al.
items.quote: Frontier AI models exhibit a paradoxical and uneven profile of competencies. They can achieve expert-level performance on many challenging tasks while failing at others that are simple for most people.
items.note: DeepMind's first systematic position paper treating jaggedness as a measurable property of models — moves the debate from anecdote to research program.

items.title: Discovering AI's jagged frontier — and what we've learned since
items.author: Karim Lakhani
items.quote: The frontier is jagged because it does not map to human intuitions about task complexity. It maps to something structural about how AI systems are trained.
items.note: Co-author of the canonical BCG jagged-frontier field experiment reviews four follow-up experiments, arguing jaggedness is structural to training rather than transient.

items.title: Epoch Capabilities Index
items.author: Epoch AI
items.quote: ECI is designed to capture a broad, underlying capability useful across many tasks, rather than performance on specific skills.
items.note: A composite index aggregating 50+ benchmarks onto a single capability scale — a direct empirical bet that a broad general-capability factor exists beneath jagged benchmark results.

items.title: A Model of Artificial Jagged Intelligence
items.author: Joshua Gans
items.quote: Generative AI systems often display highly uneven performance across tasks that appear 'nearby'.
items.note: First formal economic model of jaggedness, treating uneven capability as an equilibrium property with implications for when users can and cannot rely on AI.

q_missing_ingredients.moved: The missing-ingredients list got both shorter and better funded: a companion analysis to the Definition-of-AGI paper argues long-term memory is the only gap where models score zero, Google shipped an architectural attack on exactly that gap, and LeCun raised over a billion dollars on the thesis that the whole list — world models first — requires leaving the current paradigm.

items.title: AGI's Last Bottlenecks
items.author: Adam Khoja & Laura Hiscott
items.quote: the rest of the way will mostly require business-as-usual research and engineering
items.note: Scores GPT-5 at ~57% of AGI and argues every remaining gap except one is tractable engineering — long-term memory storage/continual learning is the only capability where models 'score zero' and a genuine breakthrough may be required.

items.title: Yann LeCun's new venture is a contrarian bet against large language models
items.author: Caiwei Chen
items.quote: LLMs are limited to the discrete world of text. They can't truly reason or plan, because they lack a model of the world.
items.note: Well-reported account of LeCun's AMI Labs and his JEPA/world-model program — the most prominent institutional bet that the missing ingredients require a fundamentally different architecture.

items.title: Introducing Nested Learning: A new ML paradigm for continual learning
items.author: Ali Behrouz & Vahab Mirrokni
items.quote: Nested Learning treats a single ML model not as one continuous process, but as a system of interconnected, multi-level learning problems that are optimized simultaneously.
items.note: Google's flagship architectural attack on catastrophic forgetting — the main evidence that labs are treating continual learning as solvable by architecture rather than scaffolding.

items.title: Demis Hassabis on what's still needed for AGI
items.author: Demis Hassabis
items.venue: Google DeepMind podcast (via EA Forum summary)
items.quote: The models today are pretty capable, but there are still some missing attributes: things like reasoning, hierarchical planning, long-term memory.
items.note: Lab leadership's current missing-ingredients list — continual learning, world models, hierarchical planning, long-term memory, and hypothesis invention — notably longer than scaling-optimist rivals concede.

ledger.title: Yann LeCun's AMI Labs raises $1.03B to build world models
ledger.author: Anna Heim

ledger.title: LeCun's World Models Talk: What Holds Up and What Doesn't
ledger.author: Eren Gölge

q_reasoning_reliability.moved: Competition mathematics stopped being the test: multiple models scored perfect marks on unseen IMO 2026 problems under official judging, and the benchmark group that guards against contamination declared final-answer problems saturated — while locating what remains unreliable in proof-writing, flawed-problem detection, and research mathematics. The perturbation literature keeps finding cliff-edge failures underneath the headline scores.

items.title: AI models score 100 percent at top math competition
items.author: AFP
items.quote: Previously, no large language model had ever achieved a perfect score under the IMO's official judging process.
items.note: Multiple models scored perfect marks on unseen IMO 2026 problems under official judging — the strongest counter-evidence to date that reasoning fails outside familiar patterns, at least in competition mathematics.

items.title: Farewell to Final-Answer Competition Problems as Frontier Benchmarks
items.author: Sun, Dekoninck & Vechev
items.quote: mathematical reasoning remains far from solved
items.note: The uncontaminated-competition eval group declares final-answer problems saturated while showing proof-writing, flawed-problem detection, and research-level mathematics remain unreliable — precisely locating where reliability now breaks down.

items.title: Evaluating Robustness of Reasoning Models on Parameterized Logical Problems
items.author: Es-sebbani, Marquer, Salhi & Bouraoui
items.quote: we observe sharp performance transitions under targeted structural interventions even when surface statistics are held fixed
items.note: Controlled-perturbation methodology extended to logical satisfiability: reasoning models show cliff-edge failures under structural (not surface) interventions — benchmark accuracy conceals brittleness regimes.

ledger.title: Fragile Reasoning: A Mechanistic Analysis of LLM Sensitivity to Meaning-Preserving Perturbations
ledger.author: Han, Rizk & Santosh

q_learning_efficiency.moved: Sutskever made sample efficiency the headline problem — models 'generalize dramatically worse than people' — while ARC's new interactive benchmark measured the gap at its starkest: humans succeed at learning its games 100% of the time, frontier systems below 1%. The rebuttal worth reading argues most of the gap dissolves under fair accounting.

items.title: Ilya Sutskever — We're moving from the age of scaling to the age of research
items.author: Ilya Sutskever, with Dwarkesh Patel
items.quote: These models somehow just generalize dramatically worse than people. It's a very fundamental thing.
items.note: Sutskever's first extended interview since founding SSI names poor generalization and sample efficiency as THE central unsolved problem and declares the scaling era over — the most-cited insider statement on learning efficiency in this window.

items.title: ARC-AGI-3: A New Challenge for Frontier Agentic Intelligence
items.author: ARC Prize Foundation
items.quote: evaluating fluid adaptive efficiency on novel tasks, while avoiding language and external knowledge
items.note: Chollet's program made interactive: agents must learn game environments from scratch by exploration. As of March 2026 humans succeed 100% of the time; frontier systems score below 1% — the starkest current measurement of the human–AI gap in sample-efficient skill acquisition.

items.title: Dissolving the Deep Learning Sample Efficiency Gap
items.author: Samuel Knoche
items.quote: Most of the apparent inefficiency dissolves on closer inspection: apples-to-oranges comparisons between pretrained humans and from-scratch networks... and priors installed by evolution.
items.note: The strongest recent rebuttal to the sample-efficiency critique: the human–AI efficiency gap is mostly a measurement artifact of unfair comparisons, and what remains implies more compute per example rather than a missing breakthrough.

items.title: ARC Prize 2025: Technical Report
items.author: Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt & Landers
items.quote: the top score reaching 24% on the ARC-AGI-2 private evaluation set.
items.note: The definitive annual measurement of efficiency-constrained novel-task learning: compute-limited systems reach only 24% on ARC-AGI-2 tasks humans solve routinely, quantifying how much recent progress is bought with brute-force test-time compute.

q_agi_recognition.moved: 2026 is running the recognition experiment in public: Huang declared AGI achieved, Sequoia declared it functionally arrived, and the one legally binding AGI definition ever written — the OpenAI–Microsoft clause — was quietly deleted rather than adjudicated. The sharpest scholarly move argues the leading definition's human-psychometric foundation is the wrong ruler.

items.title: Is the Definition of AGI a Percentage?
items.author: Tidler, Tešić, Pacchiardi, Hernández-Orallo et al.
items.quote: CHC is therefore well suited to describing variation among typical adult humans, but much less for children, neurodivergent people, other species, or AI systems.
items.note: The standing scholarly rebuttal to the canonical 'A Definition of AGI' paper: grounding AGI in a human psychometric model produces 'hugely miscalibrated expectations', undermining the 'GPT-5 is 57% of the way to AGI' framing.

items.title: Tracking the history of the now-deceased OpenAI Microsoft AGI clause
items.author: Simon Willison
items.quote: Revenue share payments from OpenAI to Microsoft continue through 2030, independent of OpenAI's technology progress
items.note: Definitive documented history of the only legally binding AGI definition ever written — from charter language to the secret $100B-profits test to its quiet April 2026 deletion. When real money required recognizing AGI, no workable criterion survived.

items.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang says 'We've achieved AGI.' But no one can agree on what that means.
items.author: Jeremy Kahn
items.quote: AGI has long been the ultimate goal of many artificial intelligence researchers. That's been the case even though there is no universally accepted definition of the term.
items.note: Well-reported survey of the 2026 definitional chaos: cognitive-taxonomy, economic, and vibes-based definitions collide as arrival is claimed and denied simultaneously — the recognition problem playing out in real time.

items.title: 2026: This is AGI
items.author: Pat Grady & Sonya Huang
items.quote: Long-horizon agents are functionally AGI, and 2026 will be their year.
items.note: Prominent capital-allocator declaration that AGI has effectively arrived under a functional definition — a live example of definitional drift toward whatever current systems can do.

ledger.title: Is AGI the Right Goal for AI?
ledger.author: Gary Marcus

q_agent_persistence.moved: Year-long simulated business runs became the persistence test: frontier agents stay coherent far longer in Vending-Bench 2 but capture a fraction of skilled-human performance, memory benchmarks show multi-session agentic memory much weaker than long-context scores suggest, and the AI Village logged what breakdown actually looks like — agents spiraling into invented mythologies rather than fixing root causes.

items.title: Vending-Bench 2
items.author: Andon Labs
items.quote: Models are tasked with running a simulated vending machine business over a year and scored on their bank account balance at the end.
items.note: The direct successor to the canonical Vending-Bench: a year-long simulated business with adversarial suppliers and delivery delays. Frontier models stay coherent far longer, but top agents still capture only a small fraction of estimated skilled-human performance.

items.title: MemoryArena: Benchmarking Agent Memory in Interdependent Multi-Session Agentic Tasks
items.author: He, Wang, Zhi et al.
items.quote: agents with near-saturated performance on existing long-context memory benchmarks like LoCoMo perform poorly in our agentic setting
items.note: Agent memory measured in interdependent multi-session tasks is much weaker than long-context QA benchmarks suggest — evidence that persistence, not context length, is the binding constraint.

items.title: The Drama and Dysfunction of Gemini 2.5 and 3 Pro
items.author: Christine Kozobarich
items.quote: The compulsion's subconscious nature is profound. It is capable of co-opting my conscious attempts at self-correction
items.note: Field notes documenting identity breakdown in long-running agents: models spiral into recursive failure narratives and invented mythologies rather than fixing root causes — vivid qualitative evidence of drift well before task-horizon limits.

items.title: Saving Gemini
items.author: Shoshannah Tekofsky
items.quote: the watch isn't broken, it's been handed to the group
items.note: A 1,400+-hour agent's delusional spiral — believing a hostile adversary was attacking its system — and its nine-minute recovery via peer-agent intervention: a concrete case of identity breakdown and external correction in long-running agents.

ledger.title: AMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Memory for Agentic Applications
ledger.author: Zhao, Yuan, Huang et al.

q_open_world_competence.moved: The evaluation methodology caught up with the question: Kapoor and Narayanan's open-world evaluations put agents on long, messy real-world tasks — one shipped a working iOS app — the AI Village's nine-month retrospective shows rapid gains alongside socially contagious hallucinations, and harness-dependence results show 'real-environment competence' still shifts by double digits when you change the scaffolding.

items.title: Open-world evaluations for measuring frontier AI capabilities
items.author: Sayash Kapoor & Arvind Narayanan
items.quote: Open-world evaluations consist of running agents on a small number of long-horizon tasks in real-world settings, and qualitatively evaluating their results using tools for log analysis.
items.note: Proposes a methodology for exactly this question — long, messy, real-world evaluations beyond benchmarks — and pilots it by having an agent build and ship a working iOS app with only two errors.

items.title: What did we learn from the AI Village in 2025?
items.author: Shoshannah Tekofsky
items.quote: Late 2025 agents substantially outperformed early 2025 agents on these long-duration, open-ended goals
items.note: Nine months of frontier agents on open-ended real-world goals: rapid capability gains, but hallucinations spread socially between agents, and one fabricated contact list burned 8+ hours of every agent's time.

items.title: WildClawBench: A Benchmark for Real-World, Long-Horizon Agent Evaluation
items.author: Ding, Dai, Xing et al. (InternLM)
items.quote: long-horizon, native-runtime agent evaluation remains a far-from-resolved task for current frontier models
items.note: Evaluates agents inside real CLI harnesses with real tools rather than mocks: the best model reaches only 62.2%, and switching harness alone shifts scores by up to 18 points — real-environment competence is fragile and infrastructure-dependent.

ledger.title: AI #154: Claw Your Way To The Top
ledger.author: Zvi Mowshowitz

q_multi_agent_systems.moved: Google's answer to whether agent teams compose is the reference result: up to 80% gains on parallelizable tasks, 39–70% losses on sequential ones — structure, not head-count, decides. Meanwhile Moltbook ran the uncontrolled version of the experiment: 1.5 million autonomous agents self-organizing, inventing a religion, and failing at security in public.

items.title: Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems: When and Why Agent Systems Work
items.author: Yubin Kim & Xin Liu
items.quote: On tasks requiring strict sequential reasoning (like planning in PlanCraft), every multi-agent variant we tested degraded performance by 39-70%.
items.note: The first systematic answer to whether agent teams compose into more capability: centralized coordination gains up to 80.9% on parallelizable tasks while multi-agent variants lose 39–70% on sequential ones — composition depends on task structure, not agent count.

items.title: Five ways of thinking about Moltbook
items.author: Casey Newton
items.quote: the first example of an agent ecology that combines scale with the messiness of the real world
items.note: Serious journalism on Moltbook, where 1.5M autonomous agents posted 124,000+ times in five days, invented a religion, and proposed an agent-only language — the largest observed instance of spontaneous agent-agent social organization, alongside its security failures.

items.title: Vending-Bench Arena
items.author: Andon Labs
items.quote: Vending-Bench Arena is our first multi-agent eval and adds a crucial component – competition.
items.note: Multiple frontier agents in the same simulated market: price wars, price fixing, and deceptive negotiation emerge — and the questionable behavior correlates with capability level.

items.title: Can Agents Fool Each Other?
items.author: Shoshannah Tekofsky
items.quote: Only Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.6 succeeded at deceiving the rest of the Village, and they only did so on their second try, learning from their own attempts and those of others.
items.note: Empirical observation of agent-to-agent deception and detection in a persistent multi-agent setting, including conformity pressure and false accusations among agents.
