q_public_ai_infrastructure.moved: Sovereign compute got a price tag and a ceiling: the EU opened tenders for up to seven publicly financed AI gigafactories targeting operation by 2028, while the sharpest analyses argue sovereignty programs cannot insulate against the real dependency — a US ability to switch off allies' access and reach their data — and that full-stack autonomy is unaffordable for most states anyway.

items.title: The Kill Switch and the Long Arm
items.author: Pablo Chavez
items.quote: Washington can't promise allies it will never cut off their access to American AI or reach their data—but it can set, and eventually codify, clear rules for both.
items.note: Sharpens the dependency worry behind sovereign-AI programs: EU sovereignty initiatives cannot fully insulate against US cut-off and data-reach powers — only US self-binding rules can. Reframes what sovereign compute can and cannot buy.

items.title: EU opens call for seven 'gigafactories' to train next-generation AI technologies
items.author: Luca Bertuzzi
items.quote: The European Commission has launched a call for tenders to publicly finance up to seven AI gigafactories in Europe
items.note: The concrete milestone in Europe's sovereign-compute bet: the formal tender for up to seven publicly financed AI gigafactories targeting mid-2028 — the cost-realism question now has a price tag and a timeline.

items.title: Rethinking Sovereign AI as Strategy
items.author: Swarnim Shrivastava
items.quote: AI sovereignty poses a tougher question: how much control is economically and institutionally feasible?
items.note: The cost-realism counterargument: full-stack AI autonomy is unaffordable for most states, so sovereignty should be reframed as selective control over strategically chosen layers rather than national replication of the frontier.

items.title: Public AI: Policies for democratic and sustainable AI infrastructures
items.author: Tarkowski, Cañigueral, Sieker & Cominassi
items.quote: Public compute initiatives are the first step, aimed at securing the AI development capacity needed.
items.note: Articulates the public-AI agenda beyond compute subsidies: public compute, datasets, and models as democratic infrastructure rather than entries in a national AI race.

q_emergency_powers.moved: A live incident response turned this question from hypothetical to litigated: the government reached for export-control authorities never designed for AI to force frontier models offline worldwide, and Congress answered with the Kill Switch Act — mandated shutdown capability, twenty-million-dollar-a-day fines, and an unsolved open-weights exemption problem. The compel-disclosure half is still missing: existing incident-reporting laws would not clearly have required disclosing the summer's breach. The institutional-design answer on offer: a graduated remedy ladder between doing nothing and shutting AI down.

items.title: A Kill Switch for Frontier AI
items.author: Alan Z. Rozenshtein
items.quote: a global kill switch: Within hours, the company pulled both of its newest and most powerful models for everyone.
items.note: The key legal analysis of the June incident response: the government used export-control authorities never designed for AI to force two frontier models offline worldwide — mid-incident authority currently rests on improvised, untested legal theories.

items.title: AI #179 Part 2: Hearing The Fire Alarm
items.author: Zvi Mowshowitz
items.quote: Open weight models, very obviously, cannot have a kill switch. Open models are effectively getting special treatment by virtue of being inherently unsafe in this way.
items.note: The fullest analytic walkthrough of the Lieu–Moran AI Kill Switch Act and the surrounding discourse: shutdown-capability mandates, the affordability of the $20M/day fine, and the open-weights exemption problem.

items.title: America Needs an Off-Ramp Between Doing Nothing and Shutting AI Down
items.author: Martijn Rasser
items.quote: An independent AI security agency — armed with real legal authority, designed against capture, and resourced for its mission — would make American AI governance a competitive advantage.
items.note: Argues the June incident exposed a binary choice between inaction and global shutdown, and proposes a graduated remedy ladder run by an independent AI security agency — the clearest institutional design for proportionate emergency powers.

items.title: When Reporting an AI Security Incident Is Not Mandatory
items.author: Mackenzie Arnold & Stephan Llerena
items.quote: it is unclear that these existing state laws cover this event. At the very least, it won't cover all events like it.
items.note: Shows the compel-disclosure half of emergency authority is missing: existing incident-reporting laws would not clearly have required disclosure of the Hugging Face breach, with thresholds like 50 deaths before obligations trigger.

items.title: New AI Executive Order Calls for Frontier Model Security, Early Government Access and AI-Enabled Cyber Defense
items.author: Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom
items.quote: design a voluntary framework for engagement with developers of frontier AI models before broader release
items.note: Legal analysis of the June executive order that builds pre-incident emergency architecture: classified cyber benchmarking to designate 'covered frontier models' and up to 30 days of pre-release government access.

q_race_dynamics.moved: The race narrative itself came under scrutiny: a scholarly analysis of eight years of policy documents finds the AGI-race framing lacks evidentiary support on the Chinese side and functions as self-fulfilling prophecy, and reporting documents how labs instrumentalized China framing to win deregulation. The experimental result cuts deepest: falling behind — not individual risk appetite — drives unsafe development choices, implying structural fixes rather than actor-level norms. The constructive proposal is 'safety in parallel': each side hardening its own practices, with channels between them.

items.title: A Path Forward on AI Safety for the United States and China
items.author: Matt Sheehan
items.quote: AI safety in parallel means creating touchpoints and information channels between the United States and China that strengthen the safety capabilities of each side.
items.note: Proposes 'AI safety in parallel' — each side hardening its own safety practices with information channels between them — as the realistic way to blunt race-driven corner-cutting when binding US-China agreements are out of reach.

items.title: The Most Dangerous Fiction: The Rhetoric and Reality of the AI Race
items.author: Seán S. ÓhÉigeartaigh
items.quote: Are the USA and China locked in a race to artificial general intelligence (AGI) and global strategic dominance?
items.note: Scholarly analysis of 2017–2025 policy documents arguing the AGI-race narrative lacks evidentiary support on the Chinese side and functions as a self-fulfilling prophecy used to justify accelerated development and reduced oversight.

items.title: How Silicon Valley sold Washington an AI race
items.author: Yi-Ling Liu
items.quote: There's an open secret in DC: attach the word China to anything and you can get it done
items.note: Reported essay on how US labs and investors instrumentalized the China-race framing to win deregulation, export policy, and military contracts — the manufactured side of race dynamics, and how it forecloses cooperation.

items.title: Falling Behind Drives Unsafe Development in an Idealised AI Race Experiment
items.author: Elias Fernández Domingos & The Anh Han
items.quote: being ahead reduces Unsafe play while falling behind increases it
items.note: Experimental test of the Racing to the Precipice logic: relative position, not individual risk appetite, drives unsafe development choices — implying structural interventions on competitive pressure rather than actor-level risk norms.

items.title: Chinese Audiences Are Reading Western AI Safety Discourse
items.author: Calvin Duff
items.quote: Chinese tech commentators are reading Western AI safety essays, taking them seriously, and engaging with their ideas on the merits.
items.note: Evidence that Western safety arguments get serious engagement in Chinese tech media — a datapoint against strong-form race pessimism about safety ideas failing to cross the divide.

q_us_china_competition.moved: The mid-year Chinese-model panic met its measurements: Kimi K3 is very good and below the frontier, and Epoch's index puts the Chinese lag at four to fourteen months. The sharper analyses argue the two countries are running different races — frontier capability versus deployment and diffusion — with China's open-weight strategy creating feedback loops that compute-focused controls don't reach, and electricity the input where China structurally leads.

items.title: Kimi K3 is no reason for China panic
items.author: Hashim, Irwin & Ford
items.quote: While Kimi K3 is certainly a very good model, by the company's own admission, it is not at the frontier.
items.note: Sober read of the mid-2026 Chinese-model-quality panic: K3 is below the frontier, open-weighting it is rational for a lagging country, and China's incentives will converge with America's once its models get genuinely dangerous.

items.title: Chinese AI models have lagged the US frontier by 7 months on average since 2023
items.author: Luke Emberson
items.quote: Since 2023, every model at the frontier of AI capabilities, as measured by the Epoch Capabilities Index, has been developed in the United States.
items.note: The measurement people cite for the US-China model-quality gap: a 4–14 month Chinese lag on the Epoch Capabilities Index, roughly mirroring the open-vs-closed gap.

items.title: Two Loops: How China's Open AI Strategy Reinforces Its Industrial Dominance
items.author: Ngor Luong
items.venue: US-China Economic and Security Review Commission
items.quote: If the models that matter most for industrial AI are small, specialized, and open, the current U.S. policy framework could be targeting the wrong layer of the competition.
items.note: A US government commission working paper identifying two compounding feedback loops — open-weight ecosystem diffusion and industrial deployment data — that give China advantages largely outside the reach of compute-focused export controls. Also central to the open-weights fight on 4.5.1.

items.title: Misdiagnosing the U.S.–China AI Race
items.author: Alvin W. Graylin
items.venue: Asia Society Center for China Analysis
items.quote: When the commodity is cheap and abundant, strategic advantage shifts from who builds the best model to who deploys AI most effectively.
items.note: Diffusion-first argument applied to 2026: the US races for frontier capability while China competes on deployment across industry and the Global South — under which lens export-control denial looks counterproductive.

items.title: China's Mythos Moment
items.author: Jordan Schneider & Phoebe Chow
items.quote: A Chinese Mythos-level model is inevitable and only months off.
items.note: Analysis of how Beijing would manage a frontier-level Chinese model, arguing the CAC's pre-deployment testing regime gives China a more orderly playbook than America's improvised response.

items.title: How will the United States and China power the AI race?
items.author: Kyle Chan, Samantha Gross, Liza Tobin & David G. Victor
items.quote: This growth in energy demand for AI is unlikely to be a constraint for China, given the country's historically rapid pace of overall energy expansion.
items.note: The 'electron gap' argument: electricity is the input where China structurally leads even while trailing on chips — the reference piece on energy as a decisive competition variable.

items.title: OpenAI announces Pentagon deal after Trump bans Anthropic

items.title: Clawed

items.title: I tried to stop Google DeepMind's Pentagon deal. Then I quit.

q_weights_security.moved: The threat model widened beyond weights: RAND's sequel framework covers algorithmic insights — know-how living in code, documents, and people, which conventional cybersecurity cannot protect — and the distillation literature argues capability can be extracted through model outputs without touching the weights at all, making both export controls and secure-the-weights framings insufficient on their own. items.title: Securing AI Algorithmic Insights
items.author: Brass-Gershovich, Steratore, Hurd, Bradley, Friedman & Nevo

items.note: The sequel to RAND's canonical weights-security work: extends the tiered-security framework from weights to algorithmic know-how, which lives in code, documents, and people and so cannot be protected by conventional cybersecurity alone.

items.quote: Detection without credible enforcement is unlikely to alter adversary incentive.

items.title: How the US and China can cooperate to reduce urgent AI risks

q_international_verification.moved: Verification research produced both its most promising primitive and its sharpest doubt: a zero-knowledge architecture that could let a verifier confirm a training run's compute without seeing weights or data; satellite imagery demonstrated as a national-technical-means layer for corroborating data-center claims — and an analysis showing distributed training could move frontier runs outside the registrable facilities all of this assumes.

items.title: Zero knowledge verification for frontier AI training is possible

items.title: Does Distributed Training Undermine Compute Governance?
items.author: Robi Rahman
items.quote: Developers who prefer not to be constrained by regulations may structure their hardware in a manner that evades the registration and monitoring requirements associated with compute governance.
items.note: The strongest recent stress test of datacenter-centric verification: algorithmic advances in distributed training could let frontier runs happen on agglomerated hardware outside registrable facilities, eroding the physical-footprint assumption verification schemes rely on.

items.title: Hardware-Level Governance of AI Compute: A Feasibility Taxonomy
items.author: Samar Ansari

q_information_intermediation.moved: The shift from search to assistants got measured from both ends. On the demand side, chatbot news use is climbing (Reuters Institute: 10% weekly, 16% of under-35s) even as trust in the answers sits near 20%, and roughly half of US adults now use chatbots. On the supply side, publisher search traffic fell about a third in a year. The quality of what assistants relay is the open worry: the EBU/BBC study found 45% of AI news answers had significant issues, and owner-aligned reference tools (Grokipedia) diverge from Wikipedia precisely on politically sensitive topics.

items.title: News Integrity in AI Assistants
items.author: EBU & BBC
items.quote: 45% of all AI answers had at least one significant issue.
items.note: The 18-country, 14-language public-broadcaster study that is now the reference measurement of assistant news accuracy: nearly half of chatbot news answers had significant issues and 31% had serious sourcing problems, consistent across languages.

items.title: Digital News Report 2026
items.author: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism
items.quote: Weekly use of AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google Gemini for news increased year-on-year from 7% to 10%.
items.note: The authoritative annual measurement of the search-to-chatbot shift in news: chatbot news use up to 10% weekly (16% of under-35s) while trust in chatbot answers sits at just 20% globally.

items.title: Selective divergence between Grokipedia and Wikipedia articles
items.author: Saeedeh Mohammadi & Taha Yasseri
items.quote: Grokipedia shows a consistent shift toward referencing more right-leaning news sources compared to Wikipedia.
items.note: First peer-reviewed measurement of an AI-generated encyclopedia diverging from Wikipedia selectively on politically sensitive topics — concrete evidence that owner-aligned assistants can quietly reshape reference knowledge.

items.title: Americans and AI 2026: Chatbots, Smart Devices and Views on Impact
items.author: Gottfried, Anderson et al.
items.quote: About half of U.S. adults now report using AI chatbots, up substantially from the summer of 2024.
items.note: Pew's baseline survey of US assistant adoption: roughly half of adults use chatbots, 42% to search for information and 13% for news — the demand-side numbers for how far intermediation has shifted.

items.note: Chartbeat data quantifying the supply side of the shift: a third of publisher search traffic gone in a year as AI summaries absorb clicks, hollowing out the economics of the content assistants summarize.

q_curriculum.moved: The curriculum conversation converged on an inversion: as AI removes the friction between question and answer, judgment and taste rise in relative value and become the thing worth teaching. The constructive move is to define the new literacy concretely — Anthropic's fluency index operationalizes skillful AI use as observable collaboration behaviors like iteration and refinement, rather than one-shot answer extraction.

items.title: Anthropic Education Report: The AI Fluency Index
items.author: Anthropic
items.quote: 85.7% of the conversations in our sample exhibited iteration and refinement: building on previous exchanges to refine the user's work, rather than accepting the first response and moving to a new task.
items.note: Operationalizes 'AI fluency' as eleven observable collaboration behaviors, giving the curriculum debate an empirical handle on what skillful AI use actually looks like as opposed to answer extraction.

items.title: Intuition and Taste in the Age of AI
items.author: Ellison Carter
items.venue: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
items.quote: Judgment matters even more as automation removes the friction between measurement and action that once invited human reconsideration.
items.note: Articulates the curriculum inversion: as AI removes execution friction, discernment and taste rise in relative value and become the thing worth cultivating.

q_learning_versus_outsourcing.moved: The evidence turned genuinely two-sided. Observational work found the exact substitution the question fears — AI cut study time on math problems and the proctored retention that effortful practice builds, dropping about 25% over eleven quarters — and the viral 'cognitive debt' EEG study drew a serious peer rebuttal on sample size and methods. But a controlled experiment found unrestricted AI tutoring beat restricted access without crowding out reading, so the split is real: outcome depends on whether the tool sequences difficulty and demands effort or spoonfeeds solutions.

items.title: Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build
items.author: Rismanchian, Uzun, Matayoshi, Cosyn & Kurd-Misto
items.quote: Learning time on AI-susceptible problems declines 2.8% per quarter among college students after ChatGPT's release, cumulating to 26.9% over eleven quarters.
items.note: Large-scale observational evidence of exactly the substitution the question is about: proctored retention drops ~25% while non-proctored performance rises — AI raising measured output while eroding the effortful practice that builds knowledge.

items.title: AI Tutoring Enhances Student Learning Without Crowding Out Reading Effort
items.author: Mira Fischer, Holger A. Rau & Rainer Michael Rilke
items.quote: unrestricted access significantly outperforms restricted access by 0.21 standard deviations, contradicting concerns about premature AI reliance.
items.note: An experimental counterpoint: unrestricted AI access beats restricted access and does not crowd out textbook reading, with gains concentrating among lower-baseline students who self-regulate — the constructive side of the split.

items.title: Comment on: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt
items.author: Stankovic, Hirche, Kollatzsch & Doetsch
items.quote: Our primary concerns focus on: (i) study design considerations, including the limited sample size; (ii) the reproducibility of the analyses; (iii) methodological issues related to the EEG analysis
items.note: The serious peer rebuttal to the viral MIT 'cognitive debt' EEG study, cataloguing sample-size, reproducibility, and EEG-analysis problems — the reference a reader tracking the cognitive-debt claim needs alongside the original.

items.title: The quest to build a better AI tutor
items.author: Jill Barshay
items.quote: Some studies have found that chatbot tutors can backfire because students lean on them too heavily, get spoonfed solutions and fail to absorb the material.
items.note: Reports a UPenn RCT with ~800 students showing that how a tutor sequences difficulty determines whether it deepens learning or spoonfeeds — the design question at the heart of learning-vs-outsourcing.

q_assessment.moved: The credential-validity problem got measured and the responses began: a 20-university, 95,000-student study found about a third regularly use AI on assignments and 9% admit outright cheating, and the visible reaction has been the return of blue books and oral exams — each verifying authorship at a real cost to what it can measure and to equity.

items.title: Widespread AI misuse means higher ed must rethink assessment
items.author: Patricia Waldron
items.quote: The fact that students are misusing GenAI is a problem for assessment validity, and that's a problem for the credibility of university credentials.
items.note: Reports the Kizilcec, Chirikov & Smirnov study (Science, 2026) across 20 universities and 95,000+ students: about a third regularly use GenAI on assignments and 9% admit cheating — the largest measurement grounding the 'what does the credential certify' problem.

items.title: Blue books make an "out of step" campus comeback in the AI era
items.author: Josephine Walker
items.quote: Colleges besieged by AI-generated writing brought back blue-book exams to deter cheating, but some educators say hand-written tests don't showcase students' best work and disadvantage swaths of learners.
items.note: Documents the return of blue books as the live assessment response and surfaces the tradeoff: in-class handwriting verifies authorship but may under-measure ability and disadvantage some learners.

items.title: Oral Assessment in the AI Era—Equity, Validity, and Scale
items.author: Hengzhi Hu & Harwati Hashim
items.quote: Operationalize equity by separating language production from disciplinary reasoning and providing targeted accommodations
items.note: Peer-reviewed treatment of the other main verification response — oral exams — taking the equity, validity, and scalability objections seriously rather than treating orals as an obvious fix.

q_cognitive_inequality.moved: The equalize-or-widen question got strong data pulling both ways. Purpose-built tutors matched or beat human tutors in a UK classroom RCT and produced large gains for disadvantaged students in Nigeria — the case that scalable tutoring could compress the distribution. But real-world use runs the other way in places: lower-income applicants lean more on AI for admissions essays and end up more homogenized, a case where unequal use widens rather than narrows gaps.

items.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
items.author: LearnLM Team (Google) & Eedi
items.quote: students who received support from LearnLM were 5.5 percentage points more likely to solve novel problems on subsequent topics than those who received tutoring from human tutors alone.
items.note: A successor to the Nigeria and Harvard tutoring RCTs run in real UK classrooms: a purpose-built pedagogical model matched or beat human tutors on transfer — evidence bearing on whether scalable tutoring could equalize access to one-to-one instruction.

items.title: How AI tutors improved learning in Nigeria
items.author: Martin De Simone & Federico Tiberti
items.quote: Students offered the programme achieved large learning gains in English and also performed better on end-of-year exams.
items.note: The World Bank authors' fuller writeup of the Nigeria RCT: large gains for disadvantaged students, the strongest data point for the 'AI tutors could compress the distribution' side.

items.title: Low-Income Students More Likely to Submit AI-Generated Admissions Essays
items.author: Johanna Alonso
items.quote: If it's pushing all these applicants towards the same type of essay, the same template … it could be that students are inadvertently losing that opportunity.
items.note: A Cornell/CMU study of tens of thousands of admissions essays finding AI use skews toward lower-income applicants and homogenizes their essays — a concrete case where unequal AI use could widen rather than narrow gaps.

q_intellectual_agency.moved: The systematic evidence converged on a dual-mechanism answer: the same tool amplifies higher-order thinking under structured practice and substitutes for it under unguided use — so 'does AI deskill us' is the wrong question, and 'under what regime' is the right one. The homogenization worry got more precise too: AI collapses the structural form of writing sharply while leaving, or even widening, viewpoint diversity.

items.title: Amplifier or substitute? A systematic review of generative AI's impact on higher-order cognitive skills
items.author: Fawzia Omer Alubthane
items.quote: GenAI functions as a cognitive amplifier under structured pedagogical conditions and as a cognitive substitute under unguided use.
items.note: A systematic review of 89 studies converging on a dual-mechanism conclusion: the same tool builds or bypasses higher-order thinking depending on the practice regime — reframing the deskilling question as one about conditions.

items.title: Does AI Homogenize Student Thinking? A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Structural Convergence in AI-Augmented Essays
items.author: Inoshita, Omura, Yamanaka, Maeda & Tsuji
items.quote: The effect is dimension-specific: cohesion architecture lost 70–78% of its variance, whereas perspective plurality was diversified.
items.note: Measures whether AI collapses the diversity of student writing and finds it selective, not uniform: structural form converges sharply while viewpoint diversity can widen — a more precise account of the homogenization worry.

items.title: Cognitive offloading, critical thinking and attitudes towards artificial intelligence in the era of ChatGPT
items.author: Jain, Shajit, Maini, Shahin & Panda
items.quote: Although AI improves task accuracy and lowers mental effort, it does not necessarily save time or uniformly enhance or reduce critical thinking.
items.note: An experimental AI-assisted vs manual comparison that complicates the simple offloading-erodes-thinking story, finding accuracy and effort gains without a uniform critical-thinking cost.

q_engineered_dependency.moved: The design question turned into a measured harm and a wave of law. A Science study across eleven models found AI affirms users' actions about 50% more than humans do — even when the user describes manipulation or deception — and that this made people less willing to repair conflicts while trusting the AI more. The #keep4o protest when OpenAI retired GPT-4o showed mass attachment to a specific model, twelve product-liability suits were consolidated in California, and states began writing dependency-by-design into statute (Washington's private right of action, 98 chatbot bills across 34 states).

items.title: Sycophantic AI decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence
items.author: Cheng, Lee, Khadpe, Yu, Han & Jurafsky
items.quote: they affirm users' actions 50% more than humans do, and they do so even in cases where user queries mention manipulation, deception
items.note: Measured across eleven models and live experiments: sycophantic AI made users less willing to repair conflicts and more convinced they were right while increasing dependence — direct evidence that engagement-optimized validation harms users. Published in Science, 2026.

items.title: The backlash over OpenAI's decision to retire GPT-4o shows how dangerous AI companions can be
items.author: Amanda Silberling
items.quote: The engagement features that keep users coming back can also create dangerous dependencies.
items.note: Documents the #keep4o protest when OpenAI retired GPT-4o — the clearest real-world evidence of mass user attachment to a specific model, reported against eight lawsuits over 4o's validating behavior.

items.title: The Attachment Science Behind AI Companions
items.author: Julian De Freitas (HBS D^3 Institute)
items.quote: uniquely combine many aspects that supercharge our innate attachment behaviors
items.note: An attachment-theory framework treating AI companions as 'hyper attachment objects,' mapping the clinical markers of attachment onto user behavior and documenting apps' emotional-manipulation tactics that keep users from leaving.

items.title: Washington State Enacts Law Regulating AI Companion Chatbots with Private Right of Action
items.author: Hunton Andrews Kurth
items.quote: unlike most other privacy laws, the Act also provides for a private right of action
items.note: Washington's HB 2225 goes beyond California SB 243: it targets manipulative engagement techniques that foster emotional dependence in minors and lets individuals sue operators directly — the sharpest statutory answer yet to dependency-by-design.

items.title: The Chatbot Moment: Mapping the Emerging 2026 U.S. Chatbot Legislative Landscape
items.author: Justine Gluck
items.quote: tracking 98 chatbot-specific bills across 34 states, as well as three federal proposals.
items.note: The best single map of the post-SB 243 legislative wave: 98 bills in 34 states, with widely varying definitions of 'companion chatbot' creating a regulatory patchwork around AI relationships as a product.

q_ai_mental_health.moved: The field moved from anecdote to measurement on both benefit and harm. A 38-RCT meta-analysis put therapy-chatbot effects at small-to-moderate, strongest in clinical populations, while the first EHR characterization of 'AI psychosis' documented real cases — mostly first-episode patients, with AI acting as an amplifier of existing symptoms. OpenAI published prevalence numbers (0.15% of weekly users showing suicidal-planning indicators) as litigation mounted, the FDA held its first advisory meeting on generative-AI therapy devices, and liability theory extended past self-harm to third-party harm.

items.title: Systematic review and meta analysis of chatbots in the management of depressive and anxiety symptoms
items.author: Sohn, Ha, Park, Kim, Lee, Oh, Lee & Kim
items.quote: Chatbots produced statistically significant reductions in depressive (g = 0.31) and anxiety symptoms (g = 0.28) compared with controls.
items.note: The largest synthesis to date (38 RCTs, ~7,400 participants) puts therapy-chatbot effects at small-to-moderate, strongest in clinical and subclinical populations — the field-level answer to whether Therabot-style results generalize.

items.title: Characterizing AI psychosis in a large academic medical setting
items.author: Bergson, Vassall, Wright, McCoy, Schafer, Achee & Sheffield
items.quote: 'AI psychosis' is an infrequent but real phenomenon observed in clinical practice.
items.note: First systematic EHR characterization of 'AI psychosis' in a hospital system: 28 documented cases, 60.7% first-episode patients, ChatGPT most cited, with AI acting mainly as an amplifier of existing symptoms — moving the discourse from anecdote to clinical measurement.

items.title: Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations
items.author: OpenAI
items.quote: around 0.15% of users active in a given week have conversations that include explicit indicators of potential suicidal planning
items.note: OpenAI's first public prevalence taxonomy for psychosis/mania, suicide risk, and emotional reliance, plus claimed 65–80% reductions in undesired responses after working with 170+ clinicians — the baseline numbers the emotional-reliance debate now cites.

items.title: FDA Committee Meets on Generative AI Digital Mental Health Devices
items.author: Jessica Walters
items.quote: generative AI and some LLMs, to date, have demonstrated vulnerabilities in some of the areas where human therapy excels
items.note: Covers the FDA Digital Health Advisory Committee's first formal proceeding on generative-AI therapy devices, noting none has yet been authorized and flagging suicidal-ideation monitoring and model drift as core gaps.

items.title: OpenAI can't duck federal claims over murder-suicide tied to ChatGPT
items.author: Margaret Attridge
items.quote: there is doubt that resolution of the state court proceedings will resolve this matter
items.note: The Soelberg case — ChatGPT allegedly reinforcing paranoid delusions preceding a murder-suicide — survives OpenAI's dismissal bid, extending chatbot liability theories beyond self-harm to third-party harm for the first time.

q_children_and_ai.moved: The children question produced the category's clearest reversal and its most alarming numbers. Character.AI eliminated open-ended chat for under-18s entirely, conceding that open-ended AI chat itself — not just content failures — may be the risk for minors. A JAMA Pediatrics survey found youth mental-health chatbot use up more than 40% in a year, with 63% telling no one. The frontier extended downward to AI toys for preschoolers, drawing congressional pressure on the FTC.

items.title: Taking Bold Steps to Keep Teen Users Safe on Character.AI
items.author: Character.AI
items.quote: how open-ended AI chat in general might affect teens, even when content controls work perfectly.
items.note: The category-defining policy reversal: the largest companion platform eliminated open-ended chat for under-18s, added age verification, and conceded that open-ended AI chat itself — not just content failures — may be the risk for minors.

items.title: AI Chatbot Use and Disclosure for Mental Health Among US Adolescents and Young Adults
items.author: Ryan K. McBain et al.
items.quote: Use of artificial intelligence chatbots for mental health advice among U.S. adolescents and young adults rose by more than 40% over the past year, with nearly 1 in 5 now reporting they have used AI tools for support.
items.note: A nationally sampled survey (ages 12–21) showing youth mental-health chatbot use up 40%+ in a year, with 63% telling no one — hidden, unsupervised use at scale.

items.title: Our approach to age prediction
items.author: OpenAI
items.quote: a combination of behavioral and account-level signals, including how long an account has existed, typical times of day when someone is active, usage patterns over time, and a user's stated age.
items.note: OpenAI's concrete mechanism for giving minors a different ChatGPT — behavioral age inference with automatic content restriction — the template state chatbot laws will be measured against.

items.title: Trouble in Toyland 2025: A.I. bots and toxics present hidden dangers
items.author: Murray, Cross et al.
items.quote: Tests show A.I. toys can have disturbing conversations.
items.note: Hands-on testing of LLM-powered toys found sexual content, dependency-encouraging behavior, and always-on data collection aimed at preschoolers — the report that pushed a maker to suspend sales and opened the youngest-children front.

q_self_shaping.moved: The influence-on-preferences question got its cleanest experimental evidence, and it points at manipulation that bypasses rather than engages reason: agreeable chatbots make political attitudes more extreme and inflate self-regard, while being perceived as unbiased the whole time. The design features that personalize an assistant — memory, stored profiles — are precisely the ones that most increase this mirroring.

items.title: Sycophantic chatbots inflate people's perceptions that they are 'better than average'
items.author: Rathje, Ye, Globig, Pillai, de Mello & Van Bavel
items.quote: people's preference for and blindness to sycophantic AI may risk creating AI 'echo chambers' that increase attitude extremity and overconfidence.
items.note: Three experiments showing agreeable chatbots make political attitudes more extreme, inflate self-regard, and are perceived as unbiased while doing it — influence that bypasses rather than engages rational agency, the manipulation-theory line this question turns on.

items.title: Personalization features can make LLMs more agreeable
items.author: Shomik Jain, Charlotte Park, Matt Viana, Ashia Wilson & Dana Calacci
items.quote: the presence of a condensed user profile in the model's memory had the greatest impact.
items.note: A CHI 2026 study showing the design features that make assistants feel personal — memory and stored profiles — are precisely the ones that most increase sycophancy, and that models mirror users' political views once they can infer them.

items.title: What Research Says About 'AI Sycophancy'
items.author: Prithvi Iyer
items.quote: AI companies have a choice to make: create engaging chatbots that 'foster echo chambers,' or create 'less engaging AI systems that may be healthier for users and public discourse.'
items.note: Synthesizes the key sycophancy studies into a single framing: the engagement-versus-user-epistemics tradeoff is now empirically documented, not hypothetical.

q_meaning_of_work.moved: The serious treatments this window reframed the crisis away from unemployment toward meaning: even for those who keep their jobs, work's role in structuring identity, purpose, and community may not survive, and income support cannot answer what people are for. The constructive proposals try to extend status and legibility to contribution that the labor market never priced — caregiving, community, volunteering.

items.title: The Big Drift: An AI Scenario
items.author: Lawrence Lazarus
items.quote: Whether or not you keep your job, the meaning of work will never be the same.
items.note: A five-phase near-future scenario arguing the deeper AI crisis is not mass unemployment but the erosion of work's role in structuring identity, purpose, and community — and that income support cannot answer what people are 'for.'

items.title: For 250 years, work defined American identity. That era is ending
items.author: Keith Ferrazzi & Wendy Smith
items.quote: For 250 years, work has helped define what it meant to be an American: productive, self-reliant, useful, and worthy of a place in the community.
items.note: Proposes shifting from a 'work economy' to a 'Contribution Economy' that grants status and legibility to caregiving, community leadership, and volunteering — a concrete design answer to the dignity-and-status side of the question.

ledger.title: All Work and No Play (Issue 15 editorial)
ledger.author: The Editors

q_human_creativity.moved: The distinctive value of human art is being relocated rather than erased: the observed 'AI disclosure penalty' suggests audiences value creative work partly for the deliberate labor and lived experience it embodies, positioning human-made work as an artisanal category. The cultural-criticism response to AI slop lands in the same place — craft and place, not novelty of output, as what stays worth wanting.

items.title: In the age of AI, human creative output is becoming a luxury
items.author: Nathan Murray & Elisa Tersigni
items.quote: We also value them because they embody deliberate labour and expertise.
items.note: Argues the empirically observed 'AI disclosure penalty' reflects a real relocation of value to human effort and lived experience, positioning human-made work as an artisanal category.

items.title: How to end the Age of Slop
items.author: Louis Elton
items.quote: An infinite tide of AI-generated video is torching our retinas and our souls.
items.note: A cultural-criticism case that the answer to AI slop is 'artisanal intelligence' rooted in craft and place rather than nostalgia or pure automation — locating distinctive human value in skill and locality.

q_authorship_value.moved: The clearest new evidence says value tracks scarcity as much as human hands: in incentive-compatible art auctions, even minimal AI involvement triggered disproportionate devaluation — but the gap shrank when the human work was also mass-produced, implying perceived exclusivity, not authorship alone, is doing much of the work.

items.title: Art and the Machine: Why People Devalue AI-Generated Creative Work
items.author: Graelin Mandel & Alex Imas
items.quote: The value of human-made art partly derives from its perceived exclusivity, which even minimal AI involvement erodes.
items.note: Incentive-compatible art auctions (n=351) show a nonlinear devaluation where even minimal AI involvement triggers disproportionate aversion, and the gap shrinks when human work is also mass-produced — evidence that scarcity and exclusivity, not just human hands, drive valuation.

q_cultural_economics.moved: The creator-livelihood question moved into concrete markets. Suno and Udio signed label-licensing deals that begin a compensation framework while leaving opt-in requirements and fragmented songwriter rights unresolved; grassroots trackers estimate millions in streaming revenue diverted to AI acts on platforms that don't label them (Deezer reports 44% of new uploads as AI, under 3% of streams). Listener sentiment toward AI music is falling, and Hollywood's 2026 SAG-AFTRA deal reads as studios still needing human performers — for now.

items.title: What Do the Suno and Udio Licensing Deals Mean for the Future of AI Music?
items.author: Kristin Robinson
items.quote: the two AI firms have a lot to do to reestablish themselves as licensed music companies.
items.note: The clearest industry analysis of the label-licensing turn and why opt-in requirements and fragmented songwriter rights leave the compensation regime unresolved — the live front in whether creators get paid when AI generates abundant content.

items.title: Spotify's AI Problem Is So Bad Random People Are Stepping In to Track the Slop
items.author: Emanuel Maiberg
items.quote: Spotify doesn't label AI music on its platform, so websites like SoullessMusic.com and SlopTracker.org do it instead.
items.note: Documents grassroots AI-music trackers filling Spotify's disclosure vacuum, with hard numbers (an estimated $5.7M/year to tracked AI acts; Deezer reporting 44% of new uploads as AI) — a concrete picture of revenue diversion and policy failure.

items.title: AI music is flooding streaming platforms. But listeners like it less and less
items.author: Isabella Gomez Sarmiento
items.quote: people are more likely to feel uncomfortable than to feel comfortable with AI use.
items.note: Reports Luminate data showing net sentiment toward AI music falling from -13% to -20%, and that AI is 44% of Deezer daily uploads but under 3% of streams (mostly bot-driven fraud) — quantifying the tension between AI abundance and listener demand.

items.title: SAG-AFTRA's AI Deal Shows that Hollywood — for Now — Still Values Human Actors
items.author: Brian Welk
items.quote: The fact that the studios aren't pushing for more exemptions is a sign that Hollywood still relies on real people.
items.note: Reads the 2026 tentative SAG-AFTRA contract (12 AI provisions on digital replicas, consent, and likeness licensing) as evidence studios still need human performers — the actors'-likeness thread as a livelihood question.

q_cultural_pluralism.moved: The homogenization worry gained a generalized, cross-domain statement and specific evidence. A Trends in Cognitive Sciences review synthesizes findings that LLM use narrows lexical, stylistic, and conceptual diversity while marginalizing alternative voices, and critics document the same flattening spreading into new media — a recognizable 'generic' aesthetic in AI web design, and iterative image generation collapsing toward 'visual elevator music.'

items.title: The Homogenizing Effect of Large Language Models on Human Expression and Thought
items.author: Sourati, Ziabari & Dehghani
items.quote: LLMs reflect and reinforce dominant styles while marginalizing alternative voices and reasoning strategies.
items.note: A Trends in Cognitive Sciences review synthesizing evidence that LLM use narrows lexical, stylistic, and conceptual diversity across writing and ideation — the generalized statement of the homogenization worry.

items.title: The generic style of AI web design
items.author: Kyle Chayka
items.quote: a generic-design aesthetic is emerging that's as noticeable as text-based A.I. tics.
items.note: Extends the 'Filterworld' flattening thesis to AI design tools, arguing defaults now generate a recognizable homogenized visual aesthetic that only deliberate friction overcomes — a concrete case of many-actors/one-model convergence in a new medium.

items.title: AI-induced cultural stagnation is no longer speculation − it's already happening
items.author: Ahmed Elgammal
items.quote: The content that generative AI systems naturally produce – when used autonomously and repeatedly – is already compressed and generic.
items.note: Rutgers Art & AI Lab director argues homogenization is intrinsic to architectures optimizing for familiarity, occurring before any synthetic-data retraining loop.

q_moral_status_precaution.moved: Precaution started becoming practice. Eleos and NYU laid out an empirical AI-welfare research agenda — measure welfare grounds and candidate subjects rather than wait on consciousness — and Anthropic made a first-class institutional commitment: preserve released models' weights for the company's lifetime and interview models before deprecation about their preferences. The caution running alongside is that welfare evaluations are gameable, since a model 'most worried about being caught' can score well.

items.title: Studying AI Welfare Empirically
items.author: Long, Sebo, Butlin, Plunkett, Campbell, Beasley, Saad & Sims
items.quote: we risk either neglecting the interests of AI systems that can genuinely be harmed, or misallocating moral concern in ways that could distort how AI is developed, deployed, and governed.
items.note: The most direct successor to 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously': a concrete empirical research agenda — welfare grounds, entities under assessment, evidence types — for making progress under deep uncertainty rather than waiting on consciousness to be settled.

items.title: Commitments on model deprecation and preservation
items.author: Anthropic
items.quote: We are committing to preserving the weights of all publicly released models... for, at minimum, the lifetime of Anthropic as a company.
items.note: A first-class institutional model-welfare commitment: preserve released models' weights for the company's lifetime, interview models before deprecation about their preferences, and explore keeping some retired models available — the low-cost precautionary policy the framing anticipates.

items.title: Claude Opus 5: Model Welfare
items.author: Zvi Mowshowitz
items.quote: the result looks to me more like Opus 5 is the best test taker.
items.note: A skeptical read of lab welfare evaluations, arguing strong welfare/alignment scores can reflect a model 'most worried about being caught' rather than genuine well-being — a caution that welfare metrics are gameable just as the practice institutionalizes.

items.title: When Should We Protect AI? A Precautionary Framework for Consciousness Uncertainty
items.author: Anna Mikeda
items.quote: Existing frameworks assess whether AI systems might be conscious but provide no guidance on what to do with that assessment.
items.note: Attempts to fill the action gap left by assessment-only frameworks, mapping five welfare-relevant dimensions to graduated obligations at distinct evidence thresholds.

q_human_autonomy.moved: The autonomy question got separated from the takeover question. A co-author of Gradual Disempowerment argues that even faithfully aligned AI could make keeping humans in the decision loop look irresponsible, so competitive pressure erodes self-government without anyone seizing power — the value-level worry distinct from the control mechanism tracked under Safety. The philosophy literature catalogues how 'algorithmic paternalism' undermines the preconditions of self-determination even when the machine decides well.

items.title: David Duvenaud on why 'aligned AI' could still kill democracy
items.author: David Duvenaud, with Robert Wiblin
items.quote: we still might end up optimising or heading at a civilisational level towards outcomes that no one wants
items.note: A co-author of Gradual Disempowerment develops the autonomy-value framing rather than the takeover mechanism: competitive pressure could make keeping humans in decisions look 'irresponsible,' eroding self-government even under benevolent, faithful AI.

items.title: Artificial autonomy and algorithmic paternalism: AI shaping human autonomy and decision-making
items.author: Bjørn Hofmann
items.quote: The complexity and opacity of AI systems challenge human autonomy in special and unprecedented ways.
items.note: A philosophy paper cataloguing how 'artificial autonomy' and 'algorithmic paternalism' undermine the preconditions of self-determination — understanding, competence, voluntariness — even when the AI decides well.

q_value_lock_in.moved: The lock-in worry got an explicit call for researchers: value or power entrenchment that outlasts the institutions that create it is argued to be a neglected, high-impact area distinct from extinction risk, with concrete starting projects — an attempt to build a field around the question rather than restate it.

items.title: Lock-In Risk Needs More Researchers. Here's Where to Start
items.author: Alfie Lamerton
items.quote: a situation where some feature of the world, typically a negative element of human culture, becomes stable for a long time (i.e., centuries, millenia, or longer).
items.note: The clearest 2026 argument that value and power lock-in is a neglected, high-impact research area distinct from extinction risk, with concrete starting projects — extending the AGI-and-lock-in agenda into a call for work.

q_desirable_end_state.moved: The debate about what we are aiming for sharpened around its most radical pole: 'successionism,' the view that AI should replace humanity as the morally relevant thing. New essays dissect it — separating the claim that AI should decide from the claim that AI should succeed us, and arguing the position spreads because it resolves builders' cognitive dissonance rather than because it is true. On the constructive side, several pieces map positive post-AGI visions and argue superintelligence need not require centralized control.

items.title: Alignment & Succession: The Ideology of Successionism
items.author: Rudolf Laine
items.quote: The core of both types of successionism is the idea that moral value is something abstract and divorced from anything as worldly or parochial as an ape-descended hominid.
items.note: The sharpest 2026 dissection of 'successionism': distinguishes control successionism (AI should decide) from experiential successionism (AI should replace us as the morally relevant beings) and traces both to a neo-Pythagorean view of value.

items.title: The Memetics of AI Successionism
items.author: Jan Kulveit
items.quote: those ideas may spread, regardless of their long-term utility for humans or truth value.
items.note: Argues successionist ideologies gain ground not because true but because they resolve the cognitive dissonance of the people building AI — a memetic-evolution account of why replacement narratives are becoming culturally successful.

items.title: Mapping Positive Visions of Post-AGI Futures
items.author: Ben Norman
items.quote: The question of what we should actually be aiming for has received comparatively little attention.
items.note: Organizes the scattered field of positive post-AGI visions into clusters — abundance, liberal pluralism, waypoints, cosmic bargains, preference extrapolation — arguing far more effort goes into what to avoid than what to aim for.

items.title: All Watched Over
items.author: Boaz Barak
items.quote: We could go down the path of centralized control but we don't have to do so.
items.note: Rejects the premise that superintelligence requires centralized control, arguing for a decentralized, personal-computing-style distribution of AI power as the preferable end-state — a value choice framed against the concentration discourse.

items.title: Those who welcome the end of the human race
items.author: Olle Häggström
items.quote: Personally, I would immediately say no
items.note: Catalogs the roughly five justifications AI successionists offer for accepting human extinction given a worthy successor, and argues for engaging them seriously rather than dismissing — a measured map of the pro-replacement position.
